News.title: Teacher accused of having sex with pupil 30 times ‘pointed at pornstar’s genitals and said “that’s what mine look like”‘
News.content:
'PAEDO' MISS Teacher accused of having sex with pupil 30 times ‘pointed at pornstar’s genitals and said “that’s what mine look like”‘

A TEACHER accused of having sex with a pupil up to 30 times pointed at a pornstar’s genitals and said “that’s what mine look like”, a court heard.

Sally-Anne Bowen is accused of abusing two boys at a North London school when they were aged 14 and 15 in the 1980s.



The teacher – then aged 25 – allegedly “engaged in flirtatious conduct” with the pupils and “engaged in sexual relationships with them both”.

Harrow Crown Court heard Bowen wore “very short skirts” while teaching chemistry at all-boys’ school Christ’s College in Finchley, North London.



She was described by one of the alleged victims as “flirtatious” and “very sexual” with pupils.

Bowen would also allegedly encourage the male pupils to “speak and joke openly about sex”.



The first boy told police how on one occasion, the boys were looking at a porn magazine when Bowen took it from them.

Jurors heard he expected her to confiscate but she instead “pointed to an image of a naked woman” and said “that’s what my p***y looks like”.

Jurors heard Bowen went on to sex with the first boy between 20 and 30 times and he believed they were in a relationship.

The court heard the boy’s mum later became suspicious and called Bowen, who denied anything was happening.



When the alleged relationship continued after the holidays, his mum called the school and was told Bowen was no longer working there with “no reason or explanation given”.

Bowen later told the boy she was leaving the UK to stay at a kibbutz in Israel, the court heard.

The boy first disclosed the alleged abuse – including details about the cafe lunches and sex – to a partner, who told him to go to police.



When Bowen was interviewed in 2015, she claimed he was a “bit of a nuisance” and “besotted” with her.

Jurors heard she described the sexual relationship claims as “just pure fantasy”.

As a result of the allegations, Bowen faced a Teaching Regulation Authority hearing in 2022.

The teacher is also accused of letting the second boy touch her breasts and kiss her during lunch at a cafe near the school.

The court heard he later read about the TRA hearing online and came forward after encouragement from his wife and family.



He claimed he was “goaded” by other boys at the school into kissing “young and attractive” Bowen.

The pupil also remembered touching her breasts and putting his hand near her crotch – to which “she would not react negatively”, it was said.

Prosecutor Madeleine Wolfe said: “The prosecution case is that when Ms Bowen worked at the school, that she engaged in flirtatious conduct towards these two boys and she encouraged and engaged in sexual relationships with them both and they were 14 to 15-years-old.

“The sexual abuse was notably worse to the first pupil who she engaged in acts of sexual intercourse. With the second pupil the abuse was limited to inappropriate kissing.

“The prosecution do not suggest Ms Bowen forced herself on either boy. Viewed superficially, these boys may have appeared willing to engage in flirtatious and sexual activity.



“But the prosecution remind you she was a teacher in a position of trust and authority. By flirting with them and engaging in sexual activity with them she exploited her position for her own sexual gratification.

“As these boys were exploited in that way, any apparent agreement on their part was not genuine consent to the sexual activity. She denied any form of sexual activity, whether that’s kissing or sexual intercourse with either.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Bowen denies eight counts of indecent assault.

The trial continues.

News.title: Putin sparks anger as he makes first visit to disputed islands that stopped Russia & Japan EVER signing WW2 peace treaty
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin has reopened a World War Two wound by making his first trip to the disputed Kuril Islands.

Fresh off observing naval drills in nearby Sakhalin, the Russian President landed on the Russian-controlled chain in the Pacific Ocean, also claimed by Japan.



Japan says it “strongly protests” the visit to Iturup, one of the islands also known by its Japanese name Etorofu.

Footage circulated by the Kremlin showed Putin touring a fish processing plant and sampling caviar.



With relations currently at a new low over Japanese sanctions against Russia over its bloodshed in Ukraine, the trip can only further inflame the dispute.

Putin breezed in telling Russian residents: “What lovely weather you have here! It’s like a holiday resort.”

The dictator later added: “I’ll just have to assume it’s always like this here.”

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reacted to the trip earlier today: “I was informed that Russian President Putin visited Iturup Island.

“The Northern Territories, including Iturup Island, are inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit.”

Japan asserts territorial rights to the four southernmost islands of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories, and argue they are illegally occupied.



Under the orders of ruler Josef Stalin, the Soviet Union seized the four territories in the final days of World War Two in August–September 1945.

An estimated 17,000 Japanese residents were subsequently expelled.

The dispute has kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.



Decades of diplomatic efforts have not produced any visible results.

Russia over the years has also beefed up its military presence on the Kuril Islands in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance to not let go of the territory.

Putin’s visit comes just a day after he accused ⁠NATO ​of ⁠infiltrating the ⁠Asia-Pacific region, and ​creating ⁠tension in ‌the Arctic.



He had arrived in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the Far Eastern island’s administrative centre, to participate in the final stage of a war exercise conducted by the Pacific Fleet, which began on August 4.

In his address to Russian servicemen, Putin said that exercises such as those are necessary to maintain readiness and protect his country’s interests and security in the region.

Arguing that the potential for conflict there is growing, he said tensions are also escalating in the Arctic region “around the use of the Northern Sea Route.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Russia has always … confirmed its readiness to cooperate in utilizing the advantages of the Northern Sea Route, within the framework of current maritime law,” the president warned, expressing that plans to deploy new weapons systems in the Asia-Pacific region pose a threat to Russia.

He went on to accuse Japan of imposing sanctions on Russia that he said were “unprovoked” on Russia’s part.

News.title: A-level grade boundaries 2026: Where to find Edexcel, AQA and OCR boundaries today
News.content:
STUDENTS have received their A-level results today, which could have a significant bearing on their further education.

Here’s everything you need to know about what your grades mean, and how each exam board gives their marks.

Where can I find A-level grade boundaries?

Grade boundaries were published at 8am on Thursday, August 13, and are available on each exam board’s website.



These boundaries show the minimum number of marks that students need for each grade.



Each exam board has its own grade boundary, and these can be found on their respective websites below:

What do the A-level grade boundaries mean?

A-level grade boundaries are the minimum number of raw exam marks needed to achieve a specific grade (A* to E).

They are set by exam boards after the exams are marked.



Boards adjust the boundaries each year based on how hard or easy the paper was to keep grading fair and consistent over time.

If an exam paper is harder than last year, the boundary marks go down. If it is easier, the boundary marks go up.

However, a student who shows a certain level of skill gets the same grade regardless of the year they took the test.

How are A-level grade boundaries decided?

First, senior examiners wait until all or most student papers are marked before setting the lines.



Boards look at statistical forecasts and compare the current student group’s performance with past years.

Senior staff read actual student work around the borderline marks to see if the standard matches previous years.

There is no limit or cap on how many students can get a top grade, so if you meet the mark, you get the grade.

Can you challenge an A-Level grade?

The request to review marking must come from the school or college itself, so you will have to speak to your exams officer should you wish to challenge your grades.

If they refuse to ask for a review, you are entitled to use the school’s internal appeals procedure to challenge that refusal.



A review can push a mark down as well as up, which is why the student has to give written consent and the school has to keep it on file.

There may also be a fee if the grade does not change, so it is a good idea to check what it costs first.

If a university or further education place hangs on the outcome, the cut-off for a priority review is August 20, otherwise the standard deadline is September 24.

When the exam board sends out the result of your review, you have 30 days from that date to appeal it.

An appeal has two stages – if you are unhappy with the first answer, you have another 14 days to ask for a hearing.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

If you have asked for a review that could change your grade, tell the university straight away.

The exam board does not tell Ucas or the university that a review is underway, but it will report any grade change that comes out of it, and the university is under no obligation to hold your place in the meantime.

News.title: Top A-level grades hit 3-year high as 900k students take exams & teens ditch easy subjects to target well-paid jobs
News.content:
LEVEL BEST Top A-level grades hit 3-year high as 900k students take exams & teens ditch easy subjects to target well-paid jobs

STUDENTS across the country are opening their A-level results this morning with thousands focusing on maths and economics in pursuit of high-earning careers.

Over 835,000 A-level results have been awarded to more than 320,000 students at schools and colleges across the country.



Maths held firm as the nation’s favourite subject this year with 107,300 students receiving results in the field.

Last year economics saw the fastest growth among the top ten subjects, up 5.5 per cent, while chemistry and business studies also gained ground.



And, this year economics and maths maintained their spots among the five most popular A-level subjects.

The majority of schools have opened their doors from 8am to 11am for students to collect their results – but it’s advisable to check your school’s website or social media.



Students are piling in to see their results and find out if they have made it into their top choice of university.

Many students have made it onto their courses with the total number accepted on to degree courses rising by 3 per cent on the same point last year.



Today marks a record high of 262,820 students taking up places so far, according to initial UCAS figures.

It can, however, take up to 24 hours for places to be confirmed at certain universities.

This morning, Ucas chief executive Jo Saxton said the numbers “paint a really good picture.”

Students who don’t meet the required Ucas points for their top choices will now face a frantic race for places through clearing.

According to skills minister Jacqui Smith the government is taking action this year to prevent university courses which are not a good investement from expanding.



For A-level results, this year saw an increase of 2.7 per cent in the number of grades awarded on 2025 – attributed to a growth in the number of 18 year olds sitting exams.

Around two thirds of A-level students took three or more subjects this year.

Of those sitting exams, 7,245 received A* in every subject they took – with an impressive 25 teens taking A* grades in 5 or more A-levels.

As was the case in 2025, the regions with the highest percentage of A Level results at A or A* were London and the South East.

The gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades and the equivalent figure in both north-east England and the East Midlands has reached a new record size.



Some 32.7 per cent of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1 per cent in 2025.

This was the highest for any region in England, exam results show.

The gap between London and each of the two regions with the lowest reuslts now stands at 9.6 percentage points, the largest since the present system of grading began in 2010.

The North East and the East Midlands had the joint lowest rate, at 23.1 per cent.

The East Midlands is the only region to see a year-on-year fall in entries getting A*.



In subjects, psychology was the second most popular with 76,100 students receiving awards for the subject.

Chemisty and Biology were also popular choices but maths took the top spot.

As well as A-level results, students were awarded their T-level, BTec and Level 3 course results today.

This brought the total number of results awarded to students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland to 1.1 million with Over 19,800 students received T-level results today.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham took to social media to offer words of encouragement to students today.



Speaking after meeting with one of his old teachers, he said: “Good luck to everyone getting their A-level, T-level and BTec results today.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Whatever it says in those envelopes, you should be proud of the hard work that got you here.

“And remember, there isn’t just one route to success.”

News.title: What time do A-level results come out today? When to get your grades on results day 2026 and how to collect them
News.content:
HUNDREDS of thousands of teenagers across the UK are bracing for a nerve-racking morning on A-level results day.

Here is all you need to know about what happens on the day, and how to collect your grades.

When do A-level results come out?

This year, A-level results day falls on Thursday, August 13.



The Joint Council for Qualifications sets the date and it applies across every exam board, including AQA, Pearson Edexcel, OCR, WJEC and CCEA in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.



This covers AS Levels, the Extended Project, free-standing maths qualifications, as well as Level 3 applied and vocational technical qualifications.

OCR’s Cambridge Technicals at Level 2 and Level 3 can be issued to students slightly earlier from Monday, August 10, but schools and colleges can choose to hold them back until the main results days.

Exams officers can see results on their systems from 12.01am, but they can only give results slips to students from 8am.

Bear in mind that 8am is the earliest permitted time results can be handed out – not a fixed release time.

Each school or college has its own specific policy on when and how students can collect their results.

How do I collect A-level results?

There are several options available for how you can collect your grades on the results day:

In person: Go to your school or college with your photo ID to collect a printed slip with your results. If you personally cannot attend, give your institution a written letter naming your proxy with their ID to collect your results for you.

Schools and colleges set their own arrangements, with some handing out printed slips in person while others use online portals or email, so it is worth checking your specific institution’s policy.

If they refuse to ask for a review, you are entitled to use the school’s internal appeals procedure to challenge that refusal.

A review can push a mark down as well as up, which is why the student has to give written consent and the school has to keep it on file.

There may also be a fee if the grade does not change, so it is a good idea to check what it costs first.

If a university or further education place hangs on the outcome, the cut-off for a priority review is August 20, otherwise the standard deadline is September 24.



When the exam board sends out the result of your review, you have 30 days from that date to appeal it.

An appeal has two stages – if you are unhappy with the first answer, you have another 14 days to ask for a hearing.

News.title: What time does Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026? When to check the status of your university offers
News.content:
STUDENTS will soon find out whether they have secured a place at their preferred university, with A-level results just around the corner.

Thursday, August 13, is results day for hundreds of thousands of teenagers – and for those seeking to remain in education, Ucas plays a big part of proceedings.

What is the difference between A-level results and a Ucas score?

A-level results are the traditional letter grades from A* to E that students receive from your exam boards.



Ucas score, also called tariff points, is a numerical value assigned to those letter grades, allowing universities to compare different types of qualifications equally.



Each letter grade you achieve in a full A-level translates into a specific number of UCAS points:

A*: 56 points

56 points A: 48 points

48 points B: 40 points

40 points C: 32 points

32 points D: 24 points

24 points E: 16 points

Your total Ucas score is calculated by adding the points of all your eligible qualifications together.

Your total Ucas score can also include points from other qualifications outside of your A-levels, such as Extended Project, AS-levels, T-levels, BTECs or music exams.



You can use the official Ucas calculator to total up your projected score.

What time does the Ucas Hub update on A-level results day 2026?

Students will be able to access their applications from 8am when the embargo is lifted.

Individual records typically process across the system between 8am and 8.15am.

However, with thousands of students logging in simultaneously, expect slow loading and be patient.



Avoid refreshing the page constantly, as this could worsen server traffic.

The Ucas customer experience centre phone lines open at 8.30am if you need direct troubleshooting assistance.

The Ucas Hub tells you where you stand with your firm and insurance university choices.

It will not show your actual grades – those only come from your school or college.

It could show one of the following outcomes:



Your place at your first choice is confirmed

You have been placed at your backup

You have been offered a changed course, which might mean a different course, a different start date or a different point of entry

Your application is still awaiting a decision

You are eligible for Clearing

You then need to check the details of the offer and do what the university asks, which may include proving your qualifications or meeting any outstanding conditions.

A changed-course offer requires a quick decision – you normally have five days to accept or decline, and letting it sit could cost you the place.

Awaiting a decision does not mean you have been rejected.

Universities sometimes take students who have narrowly missed an offer, so it is worth getting on the phone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Students can only use Clearing once their status says they are eligible, or when they have formally declined or released themselves from a place they are holding.



Clearing choices will become available to students from 1pm on results day.

News.title: Dad charged with murder of daughter Minnie Merriman, 9, in Arbroath due in court today
News.content:
A DAD charged with murdering nine-year-old schoolgirl Minnie Merriman in Arbroath is due to appear in court again today.

Christopher Rice, 35, is alleged to have killed his daughter, who was found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town on August 3.



He was charged in connection with her alleged murder and initially appeared at Forfar Sheriff Court last week.

Rice, from West Yorkshire, was led into the court in cuffs by officers on August 5.



He made no plea and was remanded in custody.

He is expected to return to the dock today, August 13, for a private hearing.



Minnie had been on a family camping trip when she was found fatally injured shortly after midnight on August 3.

Emergency services raced to the Elliot Industrial Estate after the alarm was raised and the youngster was rushed to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, where she later died.

We previously reported how Minnie was discovered after the family’s camping trip led them to pitch a tent within the estate.

Witnesses told of their surprise at the family’s makeshift campsite, less than a mile from the seafront, after they were seen cooking on an outdoor stove just hours before Minnie was found injured.



Minnie was rushed to hospital along with three other patients before she died.

In a tribute following her death Minnie’s devastated family described her as their “beautiful and brave Minnie Moo”.

Minnie’s heartbroken mum Laurie Eve Merriman left a devastating tribute at the scene in the days that followed, saying she will be “eternally connected” to her daughter.

A note from the mum read: “To my darling Minnie Moo.

“Wherever you are, we’re still connected eternally.



“I love you my girl.

“Mammy will carry your strength always.”

More to follow…

News.title: Once-in-a-generation solar eclipse wows millions in UK and Europe
News.content:
The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the Universe is.

News.title: Watch: Moment 'surreal' solar eclipse witnessed in UK and Europe
News.content:
Millions of people across Europe and the UK witnessed the most significant solar eclipse since 1999 on Wednesday.

For the UK, more than 90% of the Sun was covered by the Moon, whereas in some parts of Europe, a rare total eclipse could be seen.

BBC science correspondent Pallab Ghosh was in Burgos, Spain, and said he got goosebumps from the spectacle.

News.title: UK economy grows between April and June but experts warn of challenges in coming months
News.content:
An added boost from summer sun and sports fixtures for some businesses helped the UK economy to grow by 0.4% between April and June, according to official data.

But the figure - in line with economists' expectations - is below the 0.6% expansion recorded in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with services sector propelling growth in the second quarter while manufacturing also grew.

The economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, but economists warn growth is likely to slow in the second half of the year.

Computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry were areas of strength, the ONS said. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3% in June. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, boosted customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves.

News.title: Polls open in Clacton by-election
News.content:
The polls have opened in Clacton-on-Sea as a record number of candidates vie to become the town's next MP.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates standing in the Essex resort - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Fifty-one polling stations have opened, covering Clacton and the surrounding towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze. The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of the month, President Donald Trump has announced.

Leavitt, whom the president called one of his "most trusted aides", will depart from her role to spend time with her young children and family - "a decision I totally understand and respect", Trump wrote in a social media post.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," he added.

Leavitt, 28, took the job as White House Press Secretary last year - becoming the youngest person to ever have the role. It was not immediately clear who will replace her.

News.title: ICE plans to equip agents with gloves that can deliver electric shocks
News.content:
Unlike a taser, which uses sharp barbs in the skin to deliver a shock of up to 50,000 volts, the gloves do not complete an electrical circuit inside the body.

The gloves instead deliver a sharp shock to convince a subject to comply using "pain deterrence", says Lt Butch Gallion, an administrator at Hawkins County jail in Tennessee.

"We may or may not deploy them. It just depends on how they act. When you push the button to turn them on there's a light that displays. The inmates understand that light, and often just seeing the light brings compliance," he says.

The shocks can only be delivered when they contact skin, allowing an officer to touch a subject's clothing, and then move to the skin â typically the wrist or elbow - if they begin to fight.

If they become combative, he continues, "then you can apply the gloves to an area that the skin is exposed. And it's an instant complier for me".

According to the DHS note, GLOVE would be used by officers and agents in Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which targets transnational criminal organisations, and Enforcement Removal Operations (ERO), which is responsible for arresting, detaining and deporting people who violate immigration laws in the US.

Some law enforcement agencies are already using the gloves but it's believed that the planned ICE purchase would be the largest from Compliant Technologies to date.

Civil rights groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), have expressed alarm about law enforcement using them.

"ICE spent the last year showing this country that they are willing to disregard the law and are too quick to use force, with devastating and at times fatal consequences for citizens and noncitizens alike," said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU.

Federal immigration agents have been criticised in the wake of fatalities that have occurred during enforcement operations.

Recent incidents include the fatal shooting of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas, while Colombian national Johan SebastiÃ¡n DurÃ¡n Guerrero was killed during an immigration enforcement operation in Maine.

ICE has also been under pressure to deliver President Donald Trump's deportation agenda, which includes meeting a daily target of arrests.

"Now they [ICE] might be equipped with a device that allows them to deliver an electric shock with their hands by pushing a small button, in a move that might be imperceptible to those watching," Borchetta said.

"Giving immigration agents a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."

With reporting by Max Matza

News.title: First 100% British chocolate bar made since 1932
News.content:
A chocolate bar has been made using entirely British ingredients for the first time in nearly a century, with cocoa from not Brazil or Bali, but Berkshire.

Created at the University of Reading, it was named the Reading 100 Chocolate Bar to mark the university's 100th anniversary.

It is the first of its kind since 1932, when Rowntree's gifted a six-year-old Princess Elizabeth the only other bar of UK-grown chocolate ever made.

Food security master's student Maha Khan created the chocolate bar by harvesting, fermenting and processing the Reading-grown cocoa.

While the UK's chocolate market is worth Â£10.4bn, it is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.

Maha told the Today programme she made the bar to highlight the challenges facing the cocoa growing industry.

She said: "It is incredible that we can make 100% British chocolate â but in the context of climate change, pests and diseases, there are estimates that 30 to 40% is lost.

"And we've seen with these heatwaves, climate change, these problems and challenges are only going to get exacerbated."

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: I lost my lovely home to road scheme that got shelved
News.content:
Roberts moved into her four-bedroom house in 2011 and spent two years renovating the property with her husband.

In 2012, the couple first heard about the A38 proposals and were given a compulsory purchase order in 2021.

Many of her neighbours accepted it and moved out, leaving her "stuck in a lovely house in a derelict street".

She said the two-year dispute over the value of the house was "absolutely infuriating", with Roberts eventually accepting Â£40,000 less than an independent valuation she had been given.

"I've lost so many years of my life to this, to the point where I was in hospital," she said.

Roberts has multiple sclerosis and collapsed in January 2023, temporarily losing the use of her legs. She said two neurologists linked her decline in health to stress.

"I think on the surface I handled it well, but clearly underneath, it was there constantly," she said.

In autumn 2023, Roberts and her husband temporarily moved into a bungalow in Ockbrook, Derbyshire, where they continue to search for a new home.

In late June 2026, the A38 project was put on hold in order to fund new defence plans.

Roberts told the BBC she was "appalled but not surprised" by the decision.

"I always had an inkling that it wouldn't actually go through, because the public consultations have gone on and on and on," she said.

"I think the indecision is disgusting. How long can it go on like this?"

Roberts said it had been "painful" to see her old home boarded-up for the past three years, and for months she "diverted halfway around Derby" to avoid passing by it.

"Those are all unique, individually, architecturally designed houses, and they're empty," she said.

"There's so many homeless people. If they're going to leave them alone, why don't they do something with them?"

The Stop the A38 Expansion Group has called for the properties to be restored and returned to use should the scheme be officially scrapped.

Roberts said she will continue to search for a home suited to her disability needs, but recognised she has probably lived in the "best house" she will ever live in - on Queensway.

National Highways said the potential cancellation of the A38 scheme remained under consultation.

It added no final decision had yet been made and an update would be shared in due course.

News.title: Streets evacuated after massive fire destroys homes
News.content:
Several homes have been destroyed in a massive fire in south Wales.

Residents were evacuated to a leisure centre after the blaze spread to five bungalows on Hazlewood Road, Newbridge, in Caerphilly county, on Wednesday.

There are no reports of casualties.

Councillor Adrian Hussey said some residents had lost their homes and would be offered temporary accommodation.

He said residents tried to put the fire out could not because it was so severe.

"The houses were absolutely gutted. Their cars were damaged too," he said.

"The streets around the area were all evacuated and people went to the leisure centre."

News.title: Arrest in Thetford migrant address sharing investigation
News.content:
Police have arrested a man as part of an inquiry into how the addresses of asylum seekers were shared during disorder linked to anti-immigration protests in a town, the BBC can reveal.

Properties in St John's Way, Bracken Road, Clover Way, Elm Road and Chester Way in Thetford, Norfolk, were recently targeted by crowds over three nights.

The man, in his 60s, was arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender and inciting racial hatred and has been released on bail until 14 October.

The houses are believed to have been used by Serco, a firm contracted to accommodate migrants, which said it was investigating allegations "relating to how address information has been made public".

The firm added it was working with the Home Office and Norfolk Police "to ensure that appropriate safeguarding measures are in place".

After his arrest, the man in his 60s was taken to Wymondham Police Investigation Centre for questioning.

News.title: Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
News.content:
Scottish Labour leadership contenders have warned about the dangers of internal feuds and briefings at their first party hustings in Glasgow.

Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra made their cases to succeed Anas Sarwar as they pitched to rebuild Scottish Labour after May's crushing electoral defeat.

Those attending the hour-long event were met by a handful of pro-Palestine protesters, whose shouts were heard during the first part of the event.

All three candidates promised to change, rebuild and unite the party following its worst Holyrood election defeat since devolution.

News.title: 'Online trolls who target me are bored and jealous'
News.content:
A woman who posts food reviews on social media has spoken out against the level of online abuse she receives after some trolls have urged her to take her own life.

Gloucestershire's Becca Stock, who has millions of followers on TikTok, said while "bored" and "jealous" people do target her online, they are in the minority.

She has shared her experience of online bullying following the University of Gloucestershire publishing new research into what drives digital abuse.

Dr Amy Grubb, associate professor of forensic psychology at the University, said posting comments online creates the "perfect storm" for abuse as the "digital environments reduce normal social restraints".

The research comes as mental health charities are reporting that online harms are having a growing impact on young people's wellbeing.

News.title: GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track
News.content:
On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.

A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history.

More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.

The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.

Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.

This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

News.title: New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise
News.content:
Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

News.title: High school footballer finds venomous snake inside his helmet
News.content:
In a terrifying incident in Arkansas, USA, a high school football player found a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice on Thursday (6 August).

The Maumelle High student noticed something unusual moving inside his helmet after warmups, telling an assistant coach that it felt “funny.”

A two-foot pit viper was found hiding behind the helmet’s padding, as the student’s coach revealed “ it had got wedged between the padding and the outer shell”.

Police officers eventually had to submerge the helmet in water to coax the snake out before safely removing it with tongs.

Animal services identified it as a cottonmouth and relocated it to a wooded area away from the school.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Chelsea set Enzo Fernandez deadline, Arsenal boost, Barcola to Liverpool latest
News.content:
Chelsea have told Manchester City that they have until Friday to submit a bid for midfielder Enzo Fernandez. The Blues have told their Premier League rivals that they will need to sepnd £120m to sign the World Cup runner-up. City, meanwhile, remain in talks with Barcelona over Rodri, who is available for £60m, while they are also interested in the signing of World Cup breakout star Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille.

Mikel Arteta has said that Arsenal’s business is not done yet, with the Gunners receiving interest in Gabriel Martinelli from Galatasaray as well as Chelsea and Manchester United reportedly turning down the chance to sign Myles Lewis-Skelly. News.content:

The CIA had “low confidence” in Iran’s threat against President Donald Trump last month but pressed ahead anyway with its elaborate “deception operation” to remove him from Turkey, according to a report.

The Washington Post reports that intelligence officials received the warning from Israel but did not regard it as “compelling,” expressing their skepticism when they passed the information on to Trump officials preparing for his departure from the Nato summit in Ankara.

The president had flown to the alliance gathering in the retrofitted Boeing 747-8 jet he was gifted by Qatar last year, only to return home via a legacy Air Force One when concerns were raised about the new model lacking the necessary security features.

However, it emerged this week that Trump had in fact only joined the legacy plane when it stopped at RAF Mildenhall in eastern England for refuelling, having been secretly conveyed to a third plane, an Air Force C-32A, inside a hydraulic catering truck, more commonly used for loading trays of in-flight meals on board.

open image in gallery A catering truck was used to smuggle Donald Trump off Air Force One at Ankara International Airport in Ankara, Turkey ( AP )

The C-32A then made a parallel flight to Suffolk while officials and journalists traveled on Air Force One as expected, assuming the president was with them.

Upon landing at Mildenhall, photographers captured Trump disembarking the primary presidential plane, indicating he had re-boarded Air Force One away from the gaze of reporters.

Explaining the decision to proceed with the strategy despite the doubts raised over the tip-off, an unnamed official told the Post: “The Secret Service has had three near misses with this president, so they’re not taking any chances. They did what they had to do.”

A former official added that the warning received fit into “a broader pattern of Israeli intelligence reporting that some officials see as designed as much to shape presidential decision-making as to inform it.”

The New York Times previously reported that CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Gen. Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned Trump against launching his Operation Epic Fury strikes against Iran in February by saying that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had “oversold” the danger posed by Tehran to him.

open image in gallery Trump's route home from July's Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey, via RAF Mildenhall, England, the first leg of which was made secure by sneaking him onto a parallel flight via the catering vehicle ( The Independent )

Trump ignored their caution and the objections raised by Vice President JD Vance to back Netanyahu, sparking the ongoing war now entering its sixth month with no clear end in sight.

The Independent has reached out to the White House and CIA for further comment.

Former Secret Service agent Bobby McDonald told The Independent Tuesday that the decoy plan had been the right thing to do: “It’s been a very long two years of both domestic – and now international – potential assassination attempts.

“You’ve got to be creative. You’ve got to be nimble. You’ve got to make things happen.”

Trump himself has since said of the dramatic manoeuvre employed to secure his safe exit from Turkey: “It’s really just up to Secret Service. I just follow what they like to do.

open image in gallery The CIA reportedly expressed skepticism about the threat against the president’s life but decided to proceed with its ruse out of an abundance of caution ( AP )

“They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane, equal safety… I do what they say.”

As the officials indicated, the president has faced three domestic assassination attempts in recent years: twice on the campaign trail in 2024 in Pennsylvania and Florida and in April this year when a gunman attempted to rush security at the White House Correspondent’s Dinner at the Washington Hilton.

Trump has also faced overseas threats, with Iran threatening Trump’s life ever since he ordered the assassination of Qassem Soleimani, the head of Iran’s Quds Force, in January 2020, with the animosity ramped up considerably since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed on the first day of this year’s strikes.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran recently revealed that the current threat level his agency faces is “off the charts,” blaming a political climate more volatile than anything he said he has seen over his 24-year career.

A fellow agent added that there have already been around 10,000 threats made against government officials and Supreme Court justices so far in 2026, a 40 percent increase on the same period in 2025.

A Spanish airport that welcomes thousands of British travellers every year is set to close for major upgrades.

Almeria Airport in Andalusia will shut for six days for work to take place on its runway, with all scheduled flights cancelled, rescheduled or diverted during this time.

The major work will take place over six days “in the second half of February 2028”, a statement from the airport reads – exact dates are yet to be confirmed.

Airlines that regularly fly in and out of the airport include Ryanair, easyJet and Iberia, all of which have been notified of the works by the Spanish airport operator Aena.

Direct routes flying to Almeria from the UK include London Gatwick Airport, London Southend, Manchester, Bristol, Leeds Bradford, Liverpool and Birmingham.

Domestic routes touching down at the Andalusian transport hub include flights from Barcelona, Seville and Madrid.

The renovation marks the first work on the runway in 20 years and forms part of a wider 19-month €29m (£24.8m) project to upgrade the entire airport, which is set to begin in 2027.

During this period, further disruption is expected, with work taking place at night between 10.45pm and 7.10am, which may impact flights.

The airport is about a 15-minute drive from Almeria city centre and close to the A7 ‘Motorway of the Mediterranean’, which connects Almeria to coastal Spanish cities including Alicante and Benidorm.

Alternative airports serving Almeria include Granada-Jaén, which is 76.9 miles away, and Malaga, located 113.7 miles away.

The news follows the announcement that Belgium’s Charleroi Airport will close for almost three months in 2028 for similar works to its runway and interior.

Flights will be affected between 15 August and 31 October during the busy school summer holiday period and October half-term break.

Ryanair and Wizz Air both fly to and from the Belgian hub to Edinburgh, Manchester and Newcastle.

Common free bet traps

Below, we’ve provided some detail on common traps that users can fall into when claiming free bets:

Stake not returned on free bets

Not all free bet offers return the original stake if your bet wins. For example, a £10 free bet at 3/1 pays £30 profit, not £40; always factor this in when comparing headline free bet amounts.

Short expiry windows

Free bets usually expire within 5-7 days of being credited, and occasionally less. Unused free bets are removed automatically once they expire, so casual or infrequent bettors can lose value this way.

Remember to always check the expiry date as soon as the free bet is added.

Bet builder or market restrictions

Some free bets are limited to certain types of use. For example, some are football bet builders only, accumulator bets or bets fixed to specific sports, leagues or events. These restrictions reduce flexibility and can increase risk.

Bet builder-only free bets often require multiple selections to win, meaning long odds, and it is the same with accas. Remember to check eligible markets before placing your qualifying bet.

Minimum odds requirements

Betting offers may require minimum odds on either the qualifying bet or the free bet itself, and sometimes both. Higher odds thresholds can push bettors toward riskier selections, while a smaller free bet with low odds requirements can offer better value.

Cash-Out and In-Play exclusions

Remember that cashing out a qualifying bet often voids eligibility for the offer. Some free bets also cannot be used on in-play markets.

These exclusions are commonly hidden in the T&Cs, so avoid cashing out unless you’re sure it won’t affect the promotion.

Wagering requirements and bonus conditions

Wagering is uncommon on free bets, but it is not unheard of. Some promotions attach extra conditions to winnings or follow-on bonuses instead.

Offers requiring winnings to be wagered multiple times reduce real value, while simpler “bet and get” free bets are usually the safest option.

News.title: Buying a new car? Motoring expert shares seven ways to make purchasing your next vehicle less stressful
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Purchasing a vehicle often feels like an overwhelming task.

Regardless of whether you are searching for a brand new vehicle or a second-hand alternative, identifying the ideal match presents a distinct challenge.

Given the significant financial investment involved, ensuring that you select a model suited to your needs is essential.

Approaching the market with a clear, well-defined strategy makes navigating the buying process considerably smoother.

Here we have prepared a comprehensive plan below to assist you with your search.

Pick a budget – and stick to it

Making yourself a firm budget is crucial when it comes to buying a car. By doing so, you’re avoiding some disappointment further down the line, while ensuring that you’re not going to be surprised by any extra costs.

Don’t just think about the outright cost of the vehicle – or the monthly payments, if you’re going down the finance route – but consider servicing, insurance and tax, too.

open image in gallery ( Getty Images )

Find a bodystyle which works for you

These days, there’s a bodystyle to suit all types of drivers. In recent times, the SUV has grown in popularity and today, it’s a style which many people like.

However, with so many niche-filling cars out there, you’re sure to find one which will work.

Consider what you need the most. Would a raised ride height make it easier to get in and out, or would an estate with a longer, lower boot be better for you? Don’t be afraid to visit a dealer and try cars out for practicality, too.

Think about boot space

Boot space is another aspect to consider. In the UK, you’ll see that boot space is measured in litres, but sometimes it’s much easier to actually see a boot in-person. It’ll give you a better idea of what you can fit in there.

If you’ve got kids, then you may want to check out a car’s ISOFIX points for car seats. How easy are they to access? Are they kept hidden by any annoying covers?

open image in gallery Chery's Jaecoo 7 model was the UK's best-selling new car in March this year ( PA )

Combustion, hybrid or electric?

There used to be a time when you had two primary engine choices – petrol or diesel.

Today, however, there are far more to consider and which one you choose will have a big impact on your day-to-day driving experience.

Petrol and diesel are still there, of course, but modern hybrids offer a far more efficient option.

Plug-in hybrids allow you to charge the car up to make things even cheaper, but you’ll have to find somewhere that you can reliably top them up.

An electric car can make a lot of sense cost-wise but, again, you’ll need to think about where you charge it up and how expensive this could be for you.

Check history

When looking at a used car, history is so important. Luckily, there are plenty of ways that you can find out more about a second-hand car.

The government’s free online MoT checker is a great place to start, and this will highlight previous MOT test results and any advisories that were issued.

open image in gallery An electric car can make a lot of sense cost-wise but, again, you’ll need to think about where you charge it up and how expensive this could be for you ( PA )

It could be a good idea to run an online HPI check, too. These paid-for checks can show if a car has any outstanding finance on it, or if it has previously been crashed and written off.

Remember, if you buy a used car and it still has finance outstanding on it, then you’re liable for the amount, making these background checks an invaluable service.

Consider a warranty

If you’re buying a used car, then a warranty could be a good option. New cars come with a standard manufacturer’s warranty, but second-hand examples often don’t.

However, with many manufacturers offering longer standard warranties on their cars, there’s a chance that you could find a second-hand model with some of this still intact, which could help to make motoring cheaper in the long run.

If there’s no manufacturer warranty remaining, then an aftermarket warranty could be very useful. There are plenty of providers, too, so take a look and compare them online.

Remember to tax and insure

Before driving away, make sure that you have everything in place. If you’re buying a used car, then you’ll need to tax it – it’s no longer carried over on the vehicle itself – and make sure that you have insurance cover in place.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

News.title: Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG
News.content:
His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

News.title: Advice, cookbooks and emergency pot noodles: Your best gifts for university students
News.content:
When it comes to sending a child or grandchild off to university, it can be tempting to fill their room with every conceivable gadget.

So to help, we asked the Telegraph Recommended Community for their best gift recommendations and their suggestions ranged from desk lamps to cookery books and supermarket gift cards.

Here are the essentials worth buying.

Kitchen basics

From cupboard essentials to electrical appliances and cookbooks, most readers say they’d gift kitchen equipment.

Thinking back to his university days, reader TJ, 43, from London, says “the main essentials are around kitchen items and good long lasting food”.

“It’s nice to have some bits to cook for others as well and to make friends quickly,” he adds.

Susan, 54, from the West Midlands, agrees, recommending “basic cooking equipment” as a key staple and “distinctive cutlery, plates and cups that are easily identified”, which are particularly useful for shared accommodation.

“A box of store cupboard ingredients such as olive oil, soy, stock cubes and spices to use when cooking,” is also well-received, she says.

News.title: Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check
News.content:
Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

Team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Ebola outbreak ‘doubling every 20 days’, warns UN chief
News.content:
Congo’s runaway Ebola outbreak is doubling in size every 20 days, according to the United Nations humanitarian chief, putting it on track to soon be the largest ever seen.

Three months after the outbreak was officially declared, the case load is expanding exponentially and many believe the true toll is far higher than recorded.

If cases continue to double at the same rate, the flare-up in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will surpass the record West African outbreak sometime around the end of September.

Modelling by one health analytics firm already predicts there is a more than 90 per cent chance that the DRC will become the largest on record.

The two-year West African outbreak grew to more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths across Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea from late 2013 to 2016.

This year’s outbreak centred on the DRC province of Ituri has already seen 4,449 cases and 2,061 deaths in only a few months.

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

News.title: Sudan exodus threatens humanitarian catastrophe in Chad
News.content:
Trapped in a desert encampment in Chad, Abakar Adam, 70, dreams of returning to his small farm in neighbouring Sudan, nearby to the village where he was born.

But Mr Adam can’t go home.

Hidden from sight, he watched soldiers set fire to his farmhouse and slaughter his livestock three years ago. One month later, after resettling in the city of El Geneina in West Darfur he heard 40mm grenades rain down on hospitals while patients fought for their lives inside and witnessed civilians executed in the street.

Shortly after, a bullet from the rifle of a Rapid Support Force (RSF) soldier ripped through his gut, and he recalls how he struggled to pull his daughter from the blood-soaked sand after her eye was gouged out by a militiaman during their escape from Sudan.

Now, sitting outside his rotting, wooden shelter in eastern Chad, just 20 miles from the border with Sudan, he tells The Telegraph that he can’t forget the faces of the blind and disabled who he witnessed being thrown onto piles of hay and burnt alive.

Adam’s story is not unique and the refugee camp where he finds himself with tens of thousands of others is on the brink of collapse.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football 2026/27: Everything you need to know and FAQs
News.content:
What’s new for 2026/27?





You’ll need to re-register

When signing up to Telegraph Fantasy Football this season you will notice your old logins do not work.

New for this season you will need to register, or login to an existing, telegraph.co.uk account to play.

NOTE: you do not need to subscribe in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football - it is free to play.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



We’ve had a makeover and Leagues have moved

Over the summer we changed game provider meaning the site was built again from scratch. We hope you like the new look and feel.

We know nobody likes change, but take your time to get to know the new layout as some aspects of the site may have moved slightly.

The most notable change is that Leagues are now created and joined below your team selection.



Back to basics

With such a short space of time to get the TFF live for this season, the game has been stripped back to basics.

You’ll notice there are no Public Leagues and no prizes for Weekly and Monthly Leaderboard winners. Assistant Manager has also not been integrated for launch.



The Fixture Tracker

Whilst the game has been stripped back to basics, you’ll notice a new fixture tracker above your team selection. This is there to help you make transfer decisions and we hope you like it.

When you see a + in the tracker it indicates how many other games start at that time.



No rule changes.

Whilst some things may have changed, the rules remain unchanged.

Telegraph Fantasy Football is fantasy football at its purest. No gimmicks, no boosts, no captains. Simply pick the best XI players you can.



Assists

However, one exception is this season assists will no longer follow Opta’s “Fantasy Assist” definition and revert back to standard assists.



Did you miss it? League Cup fixtures and five more transfers

In case you missed it last year, this season will also feature League Cup fixtures meaning all competitive domestic football containing Premier League fixtures will count towards your Telegraph Fantasy Football points tally.

Why the change? Well for years the general advice early in the season is to hold onto your transfers and we thought that was getting a bit stale. With League Cup fixtures starting as early as Game Week 3 some seasons, you’d be a fool not to take advantage of some fixture gains against lower-league opposition.

To help with the additional fixtures we have also added five more transfers to your season total.



Paid leagues are no more

Unfortunately Plucky Paid Leagues are not integrated this season.



Three new teams

Ipswich are no strangers to Telegraph Fantasy Football as they both return from relegations in 2025. They bring with them a host of talent including two big names you might recognise, including Jaden Philogene (£2.9m) and Leif Davis (£2.6m).

It has been a fair few years since Hull City (2016/17) and Coventry City (2000/01) last featured in Telegraph Fantasy Football - memories may even flood back of posting in your transfers for the Sky Blues’ players. Both clubs are favourites to go down, but with some exciting signings like Tzolakis (£2.5m) and Thomas-Asante (£2.7m) they will certainly put up a fight.

Start creating your team >



FAQs





When does Telegraph Fantasy Football start?

The 2026/27 edition of Telegraph Fantasy Football will launch in the two weeks leading up to the start of the Premier League. The scoring will commence on Friday August 21, 2026 at 8pm when the Premier League champions Arsenal host Coventry.



How do I register for Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You will need to create a new, or use your existing telegraph.co.uk account in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football. Simply click “SIGN UP”, then “Continue with Telegraph” and you will be temporarily taken to telegraph.co.uk to login with your existing Telegraph account or create a new account, before automatically returning back to the Telegraph Fantasy Football site.

Note: this account is not the same as your account from previous Telegraph Fantasy Football seasons.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



How much does it cost to play Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Telegraph Fantasy Football is completely free to play. All managers compete for the £5,000 prize pool as well the chance to challenge friends, family, colleagues and fellow managers in private mini-leagues.



How many players can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You only have to pick a squad of XI players in Telegraph Fantasy Football. With no bench to rely on, finding players who get minutes on the pitch is key and we help you out there by allowing transfers right up until every kick-off.



How many teams can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can create up to five teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football with a budget of £50m for each, meaning you have a better chance of being in contention for the prizes come the end of the season if some of your selections prove to be unsuccessful.



How many transfers can I make in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Up until the first game on Friday August 21, 2025, there is a transfer amnesty, meaning you can make as many changes as you like. After the season has started you have 45 transfers for the whole campaign with a maximum of five per Game Week (00:00 Tuesday to 23:59 Monday).





How do I join a private league in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Leagues have now moved below your team selection.

This should make it easier for managers to see which league the team is in that they are making changes to.

To join a league click “Join a league” and then add the 6 digit code that the League Chairman will have access to.

To create a league click “Create a league”, name the league and then copy the league code generated to share with your fellow managers.

League Chairmen will have the ability to lock and unlock a league to new joiners.



Do ALL Cup games count in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Yes. All League Cup fixtures plus all FA Cup games involving Premier League sides count towards your TFF points tally. This adds a great dimension to the game as you will want to load your teams with players who make the latter stages for an advantage over your competitors. However, one thing to note is that penalty shoot-outs do not count towards your score.



How many players are in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can expect to compete against more than 100,000 other teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football – a vast but tight-knit community of players where you have every chance of winning one of our many prizes on offer throughout the year.

We aim to include every player in a squad who has a chance of getting some game time. From time to time we may miss a youngster on debut, but rest assured they will soon be added to the player list and feel free to let us know on Facebook or Twitter if you feel someone is missing.

Having technical issues with TFF? Check our Troubleshooting page for help.



What else do I need to know?



Get your strategy right. Getting the balance of your team right can be a tricky business, especially with limited funds, but there are a few tried and trusted methods that will stand you in good stead:



Pick regular starters

Okay, so this isn’t always straightforward in the world of squad rotation where world-class players routinely find themselves sitting on the bench. That said, there are certain players who, if fit, are almost always the first name on the team sheet. Think Bruno Fernandes at Manchester United, Jordan Pickford for Everton and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.



Find a couple of budget ‘gems’

Igor Thiago, Nico O’Reilly and James Garner were among a crop of players who began last term in the ‘unfancied’ category and were must-have ‘enablers’ by the time the season was over. If you’re able to identify one or two of this type of player early in the season, you could be on to a winner.



Be transfer savvy

We’ve all been there – you spend hours selecting your team for the big kick-off then half of them don’t start, the other half have stinkers and your star striker gets a season-ending injury. If you do get off to a slow start, don’t panic. Lurching from one strategy to another could do more harm than good, wasting precious transfers in the process. Trust your instincts, tweak where necessary and the points will come.



Read our weekly Selection Guide

The best advice comes from experts at the Fantasy Football Hub who make our weekly selection guide a prolific source of Telegraph Fantasy Football tips and Telegraph Fantasy Football match facts.

If you subscribe to the weekly newsletter this will hit your inbox on Friday around lunchtime; alternatively it can be found on our social channels or Telegraph Fantasy Football content hub.



Telegraph Fantasy Football Player List

We aim to keep our player list up to date with all comings and goings in the transfer window and the first place to look is our trusted Stats Centre. However, if you fancy yourself as a bit of a Telegraph Fantasy Football expert like the team at Fantasy Football Hub, you can find a player list below in a spreadsheet format so you can do your own analysis.

On the document simply click “file”, then “make a copy” and you will have your own version of the player list at that time to edit as you please.



Download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App

Never miss a chance to make a transfer and download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App which is available on iOS and Android.





You can follow the latest Telegraph Fantasy Football news and discussions throughout the year on Facebook, Twitter and Fantasy Football Content Hub.

Sports.title: Gold medallist Thomas chases 'own legacy' after AJ comparisons
Sports.content:
Commonwealth Games gold medallist Damar Thomas wants to create his "own legacy" after being compared to former Team GB super-heavyweight stars following his triumph in Glasgow.

The boxer followed in the footsteps of Joe Joyce, Frazer Clarke and Delicious Orie when he beat India's Narender Berwal via unanimous decision to win gold in the super-heavyweight category.

Standing at 6ft 6in, Thomas has earned inevitable comparisons with Anthony Joshua and represents one of the great hopes for the future of British heavyweight boxing.

The 21-year-old, who is targeting success at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, is unfazed by such comparisons and insists he is focused on his own development.

"Yeah, it's a great feeling [to win gold]. I managed to add my name to the British heavyweights that won the Commonwealth [gold]," he said.

Image: Thomas is aiming for gold at the LA Olympics in 2028

"Hopefully in LA I'll be able to add my name to those great heavyweights that managed to get Olympic gold.

Image: Thomas brushed off comparisons with Anthony Joshua

"I'm just in my own race at the minute and taking it in my own strides. I'm not comparing myself to anyone. I'm doing everything at my own pace, which is great. What I want to do is create my own legacy, which is a good feeling."

Thomas demonstrated significant boxing IQ in his 5-0 victory over Berwal, marking his 11th consecutive win in a run that extends back to November.

"My main asset is my feet and my speed," Thomas said.

"That's what works for me with these heavyweights, because a lot of these heavyweights rely on one shot. I don't rely on that, so it's great."

Image: Thomas has not lost a fight since November 2025

While Thomas' main ambition for now is to remain amateur and win gold in LA, he has his sights set on becoming a professional after the games in 2028.

"First, I want to tick off that box with LA. I'm taking one tournament at a time," he added.

"It's a marathon, not a sprint. And I'm just taking everything at my own pace.

"The main goal is the Olympics. Until then, I'm thinking about Olympics and nothing else. But after the Olympics, I'll definitely turn professional."

Sports.title: Jodar's bid for history halted in Nakashima defeat as Rybakina beats Gauff
Sports.content:
Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar's bid for ATP Tour rankings history was put on hold after he was beaten by Brandon Nakashima in the semi-finals of the Canadian Open.

Jodar, 19, had been hoping to make history in the Montreal for the fastest rise into the top 10 of men's tennis but his attempt to make a first Masters 1000 final was ended in straight sets by American Nakashima.

Nakashima, the 28th seed, had never previously made it past the third round at the tournament but was too strong for Jodar in a 7-6 (7-3), 6-4 triumph.

Jodar saved four match points before Nakashima finally converted his fifth to overcome the world No 15 in two hours and two minutes of play on IGA Stadium.

"Going into the tournament, I knew I was playing at a really high level, so I knew that I could get a go on a deep run here," said Nakashima.

"Obviously, wasn't thinking about the final or anything."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Ben Shelton against Learner Tien from the Canadian Open.

Nakashima will face defending champion Ben Shelton in an all-American final on Friday, live on Sky Sports Tennis.

Shelton beat compatriot Learner Tien in the night's second semi-final and said afterwards: "Super happy with the performance.

"Learner is a guy who presents me with a lot of problems in my game. A tough challenge to overcome.

"To get a win over him in the fashion that I did, I'm super pleased with that."

Rybakina fights back to beat Gauff to set up Swiatek final

At the women's semi-finals in Toronto, second-seeded Elena Rybakina beat fourth-seeded Coco Gauff 5-7, 6-2, 6-2 to book her place in the final.

Rybakina will play seventh-seeded Iga Swiatek on Thursday night after the Pole saw off ninth-seeded Elina Svitolina 6-3, 1-6, 6-3.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Canadian Open match between Iga Swiatek and Elina Svitolina.

The 6ft Rybakina finished off Gauff just before 1am local time to bring the rain-delayed night session to a close. The Kazakh has won the Australian Open and Stuttgart titles this year, taking her career tally to 13 titles.
