Sports.title: Today on Sky Sports Racing: Windsor and Lingfield feature on Thursday
Sports.content:
Windsor and Lingfield play host to Thursday evening's action - live on Sky Sports Racing.

7.41 Windsor - Law Court and City Of Poets head the field

Law Court and City Of Poets clash with an in-form trio in the RIP Susan Procter Memorial Handicap.

City Of Poets was building a progressive profile before slightly disappointing in the Coral Challenge on Eclipse day last month. He was partially hampered that day and the form of that race is very strong, so the drop back in class and step up in trip may see James Tate's representative bounce back to form.

A similar angle applies to Law Court, who ran on in a slowly-run competitive mile handicap at Glorious Goodwood and will certainly hold strong claims up in trip. His previous two showings at Sandown, which included a victory on Brigadier Gerard night, would give backers confidence going into this assignment.

In-form trio A Major Payne, Bold Impact and Parlando all won nicely last time out and remain on potentially handy marks, with the first runner winning in particularly taking fashion over the course and distance. That performance suggests the rise in class should not prevent him from staking a bold claim under Billy Loughnane, who is chasing his maiden jockeys' championship crown.

King's Code cannot be ruled out back down in class considering his Chester success last month, as Auld Toon Loon returns to his last winning mark over course and distance last August after finishing a creditable eighth in the John Smith's Cup.

Box To Box may find it tough on firmer ground after 11 months off the track, although he does remain on a competitive mark.

7.11 Windsor - Waterford Castle opposes Amo's expensive recruit

The highly-tried Waterford Castle pitches himself in calmer waters, facing Amo Racing's Partying - who was bought for 4.4m guineas - in the Matchbook Betting Exchange Supporting UK Racing Maiden Stakes.

The George Boughey-trained Waterford Castle is the only horse in here with a rating and comes to Windsor a 10-race maiden. The base form would suggest he is not very good but he has arguably just bumped into quite a few nice types in ultra-competitive races thus far.

His first two starts this year resulted in being turned over at odds-on, but the winner of the second contest won a valuable race at Sandown subsequently. This gelding finished second behind future Shergar Cup winner Archers Bay and managed to finish in mid-division in Royal Ascot's King George V Stakes - which reads very well given the winner Enceladus has since won a Group Three and the second Al Azd bolted up at Ascot next time out (earning a rating of 109).

The fly in the ointment could be Partying. This Frankel filly out of Aljazzi is an unknown quantity and should be watched in the market on debut. Of the others, Thatcham could be of interest returning from a break. Richard Hannon's charge was never in the race at Southwell the last day but could fare better on turf with Pat Dobbs booked.

7.28 Lingfield - Shangri La opposes Neswick

Shangri La opposes the eye-catching Neswick in Lingfield's Become a Friend of Racing Welfare Fillies' Novice Stakes.

The Kirsten Rausing-owned three-year-old bids to break her maiden tag following a creditable reappearance at Wolverhampton, where she placed fifth on handicap debut. This daughter of St Mark's Basilica could benefit from the step down in trip with Callum Shepherd in the plate. Her breeding suggests she will both do better at middle distances and develop with age and she sets the standard, dropping back into a novice.

The John and Thady Gosden-trained Dove Tale improved on her first start at three just a week ago, managing to place under Rab Havlin at Kempton. A half-sister to German Derby runner-up Diamond Dove, this filly could have more to offer.

Despite Neswick's modest pedigree, she shaped extremely well over course and distance on debut and can provide stiff opposition, especially if coming on for the run.

Best of the rest

Remaining at Lingfield, Kaaranah seeks a hat-trick in the opening Free Tips On attheraces.com Handicap (5.23pm). John Butler's charge has been nudged up 4lb to a mark of 74 but could go in again up against the likes of Alice De Clare and Barbury Boy.

At Windsor, the well-handicapped Great Chieftain aims to get back on track up against Colourband in the Matchbook Loves Racing Handicap (6.41pm) before Mythological Star looks to record a third consecutive win in the Classic Golden Music Group 10th Anniversary Handicap following a success at the track on Monday.

Sports.title: Where would Antonelli rank among surprise F1 title winners?
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli is on course to become Formula 1’s youngest-ever world champion, but where would the Mercedes driver’s triumph rank among the sport’s biggest surprise title wins in recent history?

With the 2026 season having reached its summer break, Antonelli has defied expectations to build a 50-point advantage over Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in second, ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix from August 21-23.

The 19-year-old Italian has won six of this season's first 11 grands prix, and his advantage makes him the clear favourite to remain at the top of the standings when the 12 remaining scheduled rounds are complete.

Antonelli's lead would have been even greater had it not been for an engine blowout in Barcelona and wheel-guard failure at Silverstone costing him a major haul of points.

However, there's still a huge amount of work to do for Antonelli to claim the title, with Mercedes' early-season dominance having faded as Ferrari and McLaren combined to win three of the last five races before the break.

Antonelli will not only have to contend with potentially not having the fastest car on the grid during the second half of season, but also the pressure of attempting to close out the capture of a maiden title.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli claims his debut win for Mercedes at the Chinese GP

Why would Antonelli winning be a surprise?

At the start of this season, Antonelli had never won an F1 race. The highlights of the 19-year-old's rookie campaign had been a Sprint pole in Miami and grand prix podium finishes in Canada, Brazil and Las Vegas.

Having been fast-tracked into one of F1's most desirable seats to replace the Ferrari-bound Hamilton at the start of 2025, Antonelli endured a rookie campaign that left many questioning whether he was the generational talent Mercedes insisted they had unearthed.

Even if, as it appears to have been the case, some of Antonelli's struggles last year were down to inexperience and the all-round challenge of being an F1 driver rather than any lack of talent, few envisioned him as the 2026 world champion.

The main reason for that was the perceived strength of his team-mate George Russell, who had more than held his own alongside seven-time world champion Hamilton during their three years as team-mates, before outscoring Antonelli by 319-150 points in 2025.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli jumps in Monaco harbour, celebrating his fifth consecutive win of the 2026 Formula 1 season

Therefore, even if Mercedes met expectations by delivering the strongest car following F1's rules reset for 2026. It seemed highly unlikely that Antonelli could make a big enough leap over the winter to be able to get the better of Russell over the course a full season.

There was also the fact that even if Antonelli could find a way to beat Russell, the likes of Hamilton, four-time world champion Max Verstappen and reigning world champion Lando Norris were - and are - all waiting to pounce on an opportunity.

Add into the mix that the youngest world champion in F1 history is currently Sebastian Vettel, who won his first title when he was 23 years and four months old, and it just seemed like a far-fetched idea that Antonelli, who turns 20 later his month, could be ready.

As Antonelli continues his quest for glory, here are some of the drivers who have previously upset the odds to become a world champion.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli wins the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix

Fernando Alonso, Renault - 2005

Similarly to Antonelli, Fernando Alonso was regarded as a star of the future going into 2005 but nobody expected him to dominate in the fashion he did, wrapping up the first of two titles with two races to spare.

Alonso had won just one race prior to 2005 but Renault became serious front-runners thanks to a key regulation change which outlawed tyre changes at pit stops.

The Spaniard built an early season lead as Renault won the opening four races and capitalised on his main championship rival, McLaren's Kimi Raikkonen, suffering reliability issues.

Image: Fernando Alonso won both of his world titles with Renault in 2005 and 2006 (Associated Press)

Alonso's team-mate Giancarlo Fisichella could not cope with the sheer speed of the then 24-year-old, who became the youngest world champion in F1 history at the time.

Michael Schumacher had won the previous five drivers' titles but 2005 felt like a passing of the baton and Alonso confirmed that by also winning the 2006 championship.

Image: Michael Schumacher had won his seventh world title the year before Fernando Alonso became world champion in 2005 (Associated Press)

Jenson Button, Brawn - 2009

Perhaps the biggest surprise in F1 history is the memorable 2009 season where Jenson Button and Brawn became world champions.

Partly due to the 2008 financial crisis, Honda surprisingly left F1 so Button, team-mate Rubens Barichello, team principal Ross Brawn and chief executive Nick Fry were left without jobs.

Brawn and Fry bought the team for £1 to create Brawn GP before doing the unthinkable - designing and creating a car which started the season as the benchmark.

Image: Jenson Button led a one-two from Brawn GP team-mate Rubens Barichello at the first race of 2009 in Australia (Associated Press)

Button, who had only won one race at the 2006 Hungarian Grand Prix, and Barichello claimed a remarkable one-two at the season-opening.

The British driver triumphed at six of the opening seven races before budget limitations saw Brawn's rivals reel them in as the season progressed.

Nevertheless, Button held on to win the title ahead of Red Bull's Sebastian Vettel, before Brawn GP was bought by Mercedes over the following winter.

Image: Jenson Button secured the 2009 world title at the penultimate race in Brazil (AP Photo/Silvia Izquierdo)

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes - 2016

Having beaten Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg to the title in 2014 and 2015, Lewis Hamilton was the clear favourite to become a four-time world champion in 2016. However, Rosberg had other ideas.

Although Hamilton only won the 2014 title at the last race, things were significantly more comfortable in 2015 as he wrapped up the championship with three races to spare.

Very few believed Rosberg could beat Hamilton over the course of a season but everything came together in 2016 for the German to come out on top.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton backed up Nico Rosberg at the 2016 Abu Dhabi decider

He won the opening four races, while Hamilton struggled to get on top of his car. Rosberg also capitalised on his team-mate's reliability issues to build a 23-point lead with five rounds remaining.

By winning the Japanese Grand Prix, it meant Rosberg could finish second at the last four rounds and still be world champion. By then, he started to think about retiring if he achieved his dream so the pressure was sky-high.

Hamilton won the final four races and attempted to back up his team-mate at the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, but Rosberg held on to finish second, which was enough to secure the title.

Sports.title: MI London's Hundred title defence over despite narrow win over Phoenix
Sports.content:
MI London had the lights turned out on their hopes of claiming a fourth straight Hundred title despite beating bottom-placed Birmingham Phoenix in a nip-and-tuck final men's group match.

As the Edgbaston crowd were treated to a solar eclipse, the visitors knew they needed to win by at least 59 runs to take third position from SunRisers Leeds and qualify for the play-off on their home patch after Phoenix won a crucial toss and elected to field.

A total of 157-6 meant they would progress if they could restrict Phoenix to 98, and three wickets in the powerplay put a spring in their step, Sikandar Raza clean bowling Joe Clarke and Richard Gleeson dismissing Mitchell Owen and Laurie Evans with consecutive deliveries to pull clear as the competition's leading wicket-taker with 14 victims.

However, a solid partnership between Jake Weatherley and Sean Dickson steadied the ship and a Tom Curran wide took Phoenix to 99 and ended MI London's slim hopes.

Dickson (23 from 17) fell lbw to Sam Curran, who then had Weatherley (42 from 31) caught in the deep as the hosts lost momentum but Jordan Thompson (23no from 13) and Rehan Ahmed (23 from 11) took them close before Trent Boult held his nerve, nailing his late yorkers to seal a two-run victory.

Earlier, Will Jacks had made a positive start for MI London before falling to Chris Wood after slicing to deep point. James Vince looked in good touch and Nicholas Pooran announced his arrival by dispatching Tom Helm for 10 runs in two deliveries, but Helm came back to bowl Vince (22 off 12) with a back-of-the-hand slowie.

Rehan then put the brakes on by deceiving Sam Curran with a googly and conceded just three runs from his first 10 deliveries, including six consecutive dots.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain and Stuart Broad reveal their choices for best local player in The Hundred men's competition, best captain and more!

Thompson took the key wicket of Pooran (36 from 21) when the Trinidadian holed out to long-off before Jason Roy (26 off 21) became Rehan's second victim. Curiously, boasting figures of 2-7 from 15 balls, the leg-spinner was not called upon to complete his quota.

Raza (17 from 13), Ollie Sykes (23no off 14) on debut and Tom Curran (17no off 9) played useful cameos but MI London's total never looked sufficient to produce the miracle they needed.

With the reigning champions eliminated from the competition, SunRisers Leeds will now play Manchester Super Giants on Friday evening at The Kia Oval, with the prize of a Lord's final against Trent Rockets at stake.

Gleeson said: "To win five games and not qualify when two teams have done the same as us is disappointing, but that shows the strength of the competition and you've got to be on top of your game all the way through - 30, 40, 50 runs can make a big difference."

Spirit end Hundred campaign with tight win over Fire

Welsh Fire and London Spirit's men's teams found themselves in similar positions to their female counterparts - unable to qualify for The Hundred eliminator at The Oval on Friday, let alone Sunday's final at Lord's.

Qualification was statistically possible for Fire but it would have meant a record-breaking margin of victory, their four wins having been close affairs and their losses heavy ones.

But that did not mean a lack of competitive spirit in front of a boisterous Cardiff crowd as the Spirit manfully defended 131 to claim a third win of the campaign.

And that decision paid off initially, Chris Woakes showing his enduring brilliance up front in shackling the powerful pairing of Jonny Bairstow and Lhuan-dre Pretorius, allowing Lockie Ferguson to benefit from the pressure applied by picking up the South African the ball after he had him dropped.

A score of 34-1 from the powerplay with Bairstow on 22 from 11, was an inconclusive start. Twenty-five balls later and it was 59-3, with the Fire in the ascendancy, Woakes having got rid of Bairstow for 34 from 19, Marco Jansen having bowled 10 dot balls in his first 15.

Liam Livingstone and Dewald Brevis, Spirit's leading run-scorers in the tournament with 233 and 212, both went cheaply, and James Coles, belatedly growing into the tournament, flickered for 29 until all 6ft 8in of Jansen leapt at long-off to flick the ball back in for Tom Kohler-Cadmore to complete the catch.

When Fire batted, they lost Matt Short immediately but Phil Salt and Joe Root cruised along, the feeling that wickets in the bank chasing a middling target would be enough.

At 90-2 off 69 balls, with Jordan Cox flexing his muscles, that thinking seemed sound but the glue disappeared with Root (31 from 31) and Cox (44 from 28). Kohler-Cadmore, Ravindra and Jansen disappeared in the last eight balls to leave the Fire just one hit away, losing by six runs.

Sports.title: Rashford absent in Leeds friendly win but still part of Man Utd plans
Sports.content:
Joshua Zirkzee and Brenden Aaronson scored as Manchester United and old foes Leeds played out an entertaining 1-1 friendly draw at the spiritual home of Irish sport in Dublin, before the concluding shoot-out was edged 5-4 by Michael Carrick's side.

On the eve of the new Premier League season, all the talk was about Marcus Rashford and his reintegration under Carrick, but the 82,000-strong crowd at Croke Park were not treated to a first glimpse of the forward in a Man Utd shirt for over 18 months.

Carrick did hint, however, that he intends to keep Rashford around after he returned from his Old Trafford hiatus in "great spirits", adding "he gives us something a bit different".

The Man Utd boss also kept a number of other high-profile stars in reserve until after the hour mark, instead choosing to give a raft of youngsters a proper run-out. Full-back Harry Amass turned out to be the pick of the rookie pack.

The introduction of Bruno Fernandes and new signing Youri Tielemans improved efficiencies late on, combining effectively to offer Matheus Cunha some pre-season shooting practice, adding to a lively attacking performance from the lesser-seen Zirkzee.

Fernandes himself was played through by Luke Shaw in the second period, much to the delight of the pro-Manchester United fanbase, who chanted 'Bruno, Bruno, Bruno' for large portions of the night, but his strike was flagged offside. He also hammered the crossbar late on.

Image: Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin heads at goal

Of those senior regulars who did start, Bryan Mbeumo caught the eye, showing impressive intensity to tee-up Zirkzee for the game's opener. Dan James and Aaronson were Leeds' conspirators shortly after to turn home their first of five shots on target. Daniel Farke's side have scored a tidy 10 goals in five pre-season outings this summer, albeit they lacked a little composure in the decisive shoot-out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Marcus Rashford recently returned to Manchester United's training ground ahead of the new season, after a loan spell at Barcelona. Credit: @rachaelandimogenmufc.

The key moments from Croke Park

16: GOAL! Joshua Zirkzee sweeps home a smart, low cross from Bryan Mbeumo.

29: GOAL! Dan James latches onto a punt from James Trafford and baits Ayden Heaven before feeding Brenden Aaronson to equalise.

46: SUBS! Leeds change the majority of their starting XI, with Harry Wilson, Dom Calvert-Lewin and Noah Okafor among those introduced.

60: SUBS! Michael Carrick sends on Bruno Fernandes, Youri Tielemans and Matheus Cunha.

80: RULED OUT! Fernandes' strike is chalked off after the offside flag is raised. He crashes an effort off the crossbar not long after.

PENALTIES! Wilson missed first for Leeds, but was reprieved when Fernandes also spurned his opportunity. James Justin's miss proved decisive as Noussair Mazraoui netted the winner.

Carrick: Rashford gives us point of difference

Michael Carrick on the return of Marcus Rashford:

"He's our player. He's come back great. I've known Marcus a long time, he offers us something a bit different.

"He's trained only two or three days and it's all normal. He's come back in great spirits. We're looking forward to the start of the season."

Farke: Trafford can be world-class

Daniel Farke on new Leeds signing James Trafford:

"He has the potential to be world-class. If he keeps going like this he will rise to the top.

"We have a feeling he can make a big difference, a top-class No 1 is crucial for the club and I pushed very hard for this transfer. I'm very happy. It was a good debut, we're all delighted to have him."

What comes next?

Sports.title: We have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade – how well do we actually know him? | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
Phil Foden says he is excited about working under Enzo Maresca, his new manager at Manchester City. We should call this exactly what it is: a very obvious barefaced lie. No doubt Foden is excited about playing football again, about challenging for trophies with his boyhood club, the new Premier League season, his new contract, a fresh start, etc, etc.

But let’s be real. Holidays are something you get excited about. Birthdays. Weddings. Amazon deliveries. The new Charli xcx album. Christmas. Playing for Enzo Maresca inspires plenty of emotions, but excitement would probably feature pretty low down a list. At best, you brace for Maresca. You steel yourself. You look in the mirror every morning and ask yourself whether you’re man enough for him. But if you’re excited, then he simply isn’t doing his job.

Hours of classroom work and painstaking video analysis. Relentless discipline on the training pitch as he drills his blueprint into your nervous system. Blunt feedback. Homework assignments to complete on international duty. My favourite bit of Maresca fastidiousness is that when his teams score a goal, the captain is banned from participating in the celebration and must instead come to the touchline to receive further tactical instruction.

For all the churn and upheaval in east Manchester this summer, perhaps the most intriguing plotline of the nascent Maresca dynasty is something that hasn’t really changed at all. Under Pep Guardiola, Foden won everything there is to win in club football. He’s been earmarked as a generational talent since he was a child, played for England in three international tournaments, embedded himself in one of the greatest club teams ever seen. He’s now 26 years old. On some level, we have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade. How well do we know him?

To take one example: it’s the year 2026, and nobody really knows what his best position is. Is he a forward or an attacking midfielder? Is he at his best central, or wide, or wide coming central? Deep, on the last line, between the lines? Come to think of it, what is it he does again? Good passer, but not really a pure creator. Good feet, but not really a pure dribbler. Scores goals, but not an elite goalscorer (with the exception of 2023-24, when he inexplicably started walloping in 25-yard screamers). Arguably not top 10 in the world in any single facet of the game. Yet still incontrovertibly very good, for reasons that have long been internalised but which still feel hard to articulate. How, after 49 international caps and 225 games in the most scrutinised league in the world, is this even possible?

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola changed where and how much he used Phil Foden repeatedly over his time at Manchester City. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

In nine seasons as his manager, Guardiola provided all the answers, albeit not always in an intelligible order. “Winger suits him better,” he said in 2022, predicting he would eventually move to the centre. By 2023, he was warning Foden that he was too much of a “free instinct” to be trusted with a central role.

Two years later, he said Foden’s best position was as a No 10, “a little bit free and close to the box”. Occasionally, he was used as a false 9. Last season, he was deployed in a deeper midfield role. (“Not a player to control the game,” Guardiola would say just before he left.)

So over the years Foden would become a kind of footballing Calpol: a plug-in solution versatile enough to be deployed for pretty much any purpose. Does this explain the sharp decline? In 2024, he was the Premier League player of the year. By the 2025-26 run-in he was essentially a passenger: unused against Real Madrid, a 90th-minute pity substitute in the Carabao Cup final against Arsenal. Two days before England’s epochal game at the Azteca Stadium, Foden was at Wimbledon watching Iga Swiatek in the third round. What happened? How does he recapture the best version of himself? And – more pointedly – what if we’ve already seen it?

View image in fullscreen Phil Foden spent the early summer watching other sports after being left out of England’s World Cup squad. Photograph: Andy Hone/LAT Images

These are questions with implications that go well beyond City and Maresca. For English football, which has spent decades trying to unlock the secret of industrial talent development, to work out how players grow and why they flourish, Foden is Patient Zero. Take a preternatural teenage talent, hand-picked from a cast of millions. Furnish him with the best facilities, the best footballing education, that money can buy. Surround him with champion players and one of the best coaches in history, at a club where there is stability and a process and he can mature at his own gradual rate: neither thrown in too early, nor held back too long, nor pounded into the ground. If you were trying to engineer an elite football career from the ground up, Foden is how you would do it.

If it turns out he peaked at 24, what does that say about the system that created him? If your generational talent ultimately can’t beat Noni Madueke and Ivan Toney to a place in the World Cup squad, whose fault is that? Foden? The media hype machine? The coach who developed him, nurtured him, showed him the road to greatness, but also played him in about eight different positions and never quite allowed him to forge his own identity as a footballer?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Obviously it’s not really Pep’s fault. But Foden is perhaps unique among Guardiola’s prodigies in that he was there right from the very start of the journey. This actually happens a lot less than you think. Lionel Messi was already 21 when Guardiola took over at Barcelona and basically destined to be brilliant. Pretty much all his greatest players were refined and improved rather than nurtured wholesale from childhood. And so Foden is a kind of player English football has never really produced in its history: a street talent adapted over years, by painstaking degrees, into an incredibly complex but essentially bespoke player, a single solution for a single team.

Foden is 26 and still largely devoid of context. We don’t know how he’d play in a struggling team. We don’t know what would happen if he had the keys to dictate a game. We don’t know what happens when you give him responsibility. We don’t even know much about his tactical intelligence, because he’s played his entire career under a guy telling him exactly where and when to run. Perhaps this explains the wild discrepancy between City Foden (17 major trophies) and England Foden (a goal on average every 18 months).

View image in fullscreen Foden’s best season for City was in 2023-24 when he scored 27 goals in all competitions. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images

Now, under a new manager, with a new midfield, Foden faces – remarkably – a make-or-break season. Bernardo Silva has gone. Rodri may well follow. Rayan Cherki is probably ahead of him in the pecking order. In a Premier League increasingly built around lightning pace and brute physicality, where does Foden fit into the new vision? What happens if he endures a third disappointing season in succession?

But there are opportunities here too. City’s World Cup players are only just returning and there should be time for him to stake a claim. A more vertical, high-energy style may just suit him. For all his kooky control-freakery, a new manager like Maresca will never be able to exert the same stranglehold as the man he replaced. For better or worse, this may just be the season when we finally find out who Phil Foden is.

Sports.title: Kvaratskhelia and Madjo show that beautiful game can wash away Infantino’s stain | Nick Ames
Sports.content:
This was an opportune night to show off some of Uefa’s crown jewels. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia knows a thing or two about sitting Fifa tournaments out, albeit through sheer accident of birth, but proved yet again that he will show up whatever the stage. It was some way to kick off a European football season when the Georgian, with a familiar exhibition of assured footwork and rip-roaring finishing, found Marco Bizot’s top corner. Given the past fortnight’s events nobody could turn their noses up at a reminder of why, through the muck and grubbiness that has thrown the sport into turmoil, we are all really here.

Earlier on, the Uefa hierarchy and guests had enjoyed their pre-match lunch inside Hangar 7, a vast exhibition hall next to Salzburg airport that houses an array of cars and craft from Red Bull’s various endeavours. A main course of Wagyu tenderloin stole the scene and, for those craving a dose of local flavour, curd cheese dumplings were served next. But the main topic of conversation on the menu brought a more bitter taste. The fallout from Gianni Infantino’s collapsed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme will cast its own eclipse over football until an agreeable resolution has been reached.

It is becoming clearer by the day that this will not occur straightaway. The chances of Infantino stepping aside voluntarily appear slim, even if he will have to front up and answer for himself at some point. Uefa has, at least, set a brisk pace in efforts to bring about his removal. There was a palpable sense of purpose on the sidelines of an occasion that does not always lure its member associations from the sun lounger. If a first day back at school is usually for reintroductions and holiday tales, this time there was a steady hum of discussion concerning the fundamentals of football’s future around Uefa’s temporary base in the neo-baroque trappings of Hotel Sacher.

In the short term there remains a live risk that the prognosis involves a boycott of Fifa-run competitions, beginning in theory with the under-20 women’s World Cup next month. How strongly that holds remains to be seen. Uefa can certainly feel confident in its own product, fronted by a Champions League with revenues that have long roused the green-eyed monster within Fifa’s mandarins. Even this Super Cup final, a souped-up friendly between the world’s best team and contenders revelling in a generational high, offered enough hope that football tends to rise high above those wrecking it from within.

A dazzling first impression on the wider consciousness by Brian Madjo, a 17-year-old striker of phenomenal strength and composure, told that the future is worth nurturing. Madjo, who had never played a competitive game for Aston Villa, scored their equaliser and gave Paris Saint-Germain’s defence a pummelling all night. The PSG matchwinner, Désiré Doué, is a bona-fide star who turned 21 in June and was similarly unknown three years ago. Sport stretches, strains and regenerates, even if it is never wise to take that for granted.

View image in fullscreen The Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin with the Somali referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the US before the World Cup. Photograph: Darko Bandić/AP

The presence of Omar Artan, the Somali referee denied entry to the US before the World Cup, was a reminder of modern-day tensions. How refreshing it was to see Artan, who officiated with a sure touch and quiet authority, given his chance after Uefa swiftly awarded him the final in June. It is what a fluid, coherent global football landscape should look like and was only ever going to be a significant win for the European game’s governing body.

Before the match a supporter could be seen queueing at the turnstile wearing a Somalia national team tracksuit top. Anyone worried Artan and his all-African team of colleagues would be spared the full elite football experience could crack a wry smile as they were lightly booed upon collecting their medals, the Villa support smarting from the correct VAR call that awarded Doué’s goal.

Back in Hangar-7, whose glass-panelled design has greenhouse-like consequences on days like these, Uefa’s delegates had sucked up the obligatory speeches and chewed over what might come next. There will be more heat to weather in the seven months before Infantino is due to stand for re-election in Rabat, which has become a safe haven for the embattled Swiss. The strength of Europe’s united front may be the decisive factor in whether, as one diner bullishly opined later, Infantino really is toast.

In the meantime, the beguiling, unorthodox and often unplayable figure of Kvaratskhelia spoke more eloquently than any politician could. Uefa and many of its allies will meet again in a fortnight for the Champions League draw, held in Monaco and generally an event that causes more buzz among powerbrokers. They must quickly find a way to ensure football’s voice continues to overwhelm the unseemly hubbub threatening to engulf it.

Sports.title: Championship 2026-27 preview: the contenders, hopefuls and strugglers
Sports.content:
Contenders

The relegated teams, naturally, will be the favourites to go back up but two have endured confusing summers. Jarrod Bowen committing to West Ham was a bonus and the quality available to Nuno Espírito Santo should make bouncing back straightforward for the calmest of the clubs to have dropped down. They brought in huge fees for Crysencio Summerville and Mateus Fernandes but incoming activity has been pedestrian, which is the only minor cause of concern.

Wolves sacked Rob Edwards out of nowhere and appointed César Peixoto for reasons few could comprehend, because why would you want a head coach with experience of success in a league when you can bring in one who has never been involved with English football? This overshadowed the positive work done on transfers, acquiring Kieran Trippier and Raúl Jiménez, two who will lead the charge upwards.

View image in fullscreen Raúl Jiménez is back at Wolves after a three year break at Fulham. Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty Images

At Turf Moor the search for a new man in the dugout was less dramatic, more of a slowburner, as Nicky Hayen belatedly took the Burnley job. He will have to cope with a squad shorn of talent after Jaidon Anthony, Maxime Estève and Florentino Luís left with the incomings creating little excitement.

Southampton may think they should not be in this league but they have only themselves to blame and will face hostility wherever they go after spygate. Tonda Eckert has kept his job but will need to justify that faith by pushing for a top-two spot. The German’s unwitting victims, Middlesbrough, will be hurting from losing to Hull at Wembley but recuperation has been aided by investment in Jeremy Sarmiento, Radek Vitek and Will Lankshear.

After surprising many with a push for automatic promotion, Millwall knew this was the time to build on success, making clever signings of young players to aid the long-term strategy, with the £5m capture of the Belgian midfielder Mathis Servais the most intriguing. Wrexham’s ownership and financial backing means they will always be talked about and having missed out on the playoffs in their first season back at this level, they will want more.

Things were very quiet in north Wales until signing Anthony Patterson for a club record fee from Sunderland.

View image in fullscreen Despite the looming threat of an FA ban for his role in the spying scandal, Tonda Eckert starts the season still in charge at Southampton. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

Hopefuls

Building on finishing 10th is a difficult task for Birmingham, who have looked far and wide for reinforcements. Their potential to threaten the top six will depend on fixing poor away form and whether August Priske can become as prolific as many believe he can, while a poor start could put Chris Davies under pressure. Roy Hodgson ended the season with Bristol City but it is Michael Skubala’s job to take them forward, hoping to continue his personal momentum after success at Lincoln. Money has not been a problem with a combined £8m spent on Lorent Tolaj and Dom Ballard, but the free arrival of Jed Wallace may be the best bit of business.

There will, undoubtedly, be a team from this category that ruffle some feathers on the way to finishing in the expanded playoffs system, bringing an additional layer of hope to the peloton. After the shambles of last summer and the start of the campaign, maybe Sheffield United have learned from their mistakes. No dreadful signings or appointments have been made, and with Tom Cannon and Patrick Bamford they possess firepower.

Stoke have thrown the cash around, most notably £10m on Ethan Galbraith from Swansea, in hope the team does not tail off after promising beginnings again but finding a consistent scorer could be a problem. Preston never give the impression of going up but turning Alfie Devine’s loan permanent implies a degree of ambition even if another mid-table finish seems more likely than a trip to the Promised Land. Another eclectic window makes Swansea a fun team to follow but whether Elijah Just or Joseph Opoku can turn them side from middle-of-the-road to challengers remains to be seen.

View image in fullscreen Preston were sufficiently impressed with Alfie Devine’s loan from Tottenham that they broke their club record to sign him permanently. Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty Images

John Eustace has instilled stability at Derby, and getting Bobby Clark and Sammie Szmodics back was shrewd, but they do not feel much more than mid-table. Building on the second half of last season under Philippe Clement is the plan for Norwich, who possess plenty of potential in Jacob Wright, Mohamed Touré and Jovon Makama but it may be a year too soon for them to lead the team upwards.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The constant churn of managers and players at Watford will catch up with them at some point. They were poor last season and finding reasons why things may have changed is difficult with Alessio Dionisi the latest tasked with the impossible job. It is evident that Portsmouth want to buy and develop players under the age of 23. It leaves John Mousinho a rewarding but complex job of balancing results and individual progress. Lincoln are great innovators, which partly explains why they have made it to the Championship. The loss of Skubala was a dent in the ambition, leaving Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw to team up as joint-head coaches, which will add an additional layer of interest.

Strugglers

The good news is that Tony Mowbray is back at Ewood Park with the aim of avoiding another Blackburn relegation battle. The bad news is that it is unclear whether he has the tools at his disposal. James Morrison is no longer a caretaker but has to oversee a young and thin West Brom squad, which does not bode well. Charlton survived somewhat comfortably in the end and they have attracted Karlan Grant back and signed the skilful Millenic Alli but they still feel like a side destined for a long 10 months. The second half of the season was forgettable for QPR, so if there is a team looking over their shoulder, they play at Loftus Road.

The promoted Bolton need Sam Dalby to prove he can take the step up, otherwise goals may be difficult to find. Cardiff, meanwhile, will be reliant on those who brought them up after a quiet summer.

Ones to watch

Mateus Mané, Wolves, 18 The Portuguese forward has already shown himself to be capable of playing in the Premier League, so may find life in the Championship child’s play. A dynamic midfield eager to attack and score goals, Wolves have done well to keep hold of him.

Micah Mbick, Charlton, 19 A fine loan spell at League Two Colchester has given the striker grounding but he will be looking to kick on and shine higher up the pyramid. He has all the physical attributes – strong, fast, good in the air – but will want to hone his technical skills.

Luke Brooke-Smith, Portsmouth, 18 Brought in from Wellington Phoenix, the winger only turned 18 in June but already has an international cap for New Zealand. A lack of options gave him an opportunity in the Carabao Cup where he soon proved his capabilities to show he already has the quality to be an asset for Pompey.

Sports.title: Coach in DR Congo banned by Fifa for 20 years for sexual abuse still training young players
Sports.content:
A coach in the Democratic Republic of the Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa in March 2023 for sexual abuse of a minor is continuing to take charge of young players, the Guardian can reveal.

Jonathan Bukabakwa, who is known as Messi and previously coached youth teams in the Limpopo and Malabo regions, was also fined 100,000 Swiss francs after a Fifa investigation found him of guilty of sexual abuse. He had also been convicted of similar offences by authorities in the DRC but was released from prison last year.

The Guardian has seen several videos of Bukabakwa coaching a group of young players at Esperanto, a club in the Limete district of the Congolese capital, Kinshasa. Several local sources have confirmed that he has been regularly spotted taking charge of groups at a school field. “Messi? He’s still coaching, you can easily meet him with his team. He doesn’t hide,” said one, who did not want to be named.

Esperanto did not respond for a request to comment but Bukabakwa, when contacted by the Guardian, did not deny that he is continuing to coach young players and even claimed he was not aware that he had been banned by Fifa. “They never told me anything,” he said. “They never questioned me or sent me anything.” He has denied the allegations.

Fifa did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. It said in the statement that announced Bukabakwa’s ban in 2023 that its decision had been taken “in line with Fifa’s zero tolerance approach to all forms of abuse in football”. The statement added: “World football’s governing body has regularly updated its regulatory framework in recent years to provide greater protection to victims of discrimination and sexual abuse or harassment.”

The case has again highlighted serious flaws with Fifa’s safeguarding processes. It is understood that the Congolese Association Football Federation (Fecofa) president, Véron Mosengo-Omba, has summoned Bukabakwa and the president of Esperanto to a meeting on Monday after being contacted by the Guardian.

“We have zero tolerance for this kind of behaviour,” he said in a statement. “We will punish anyone involved in this kind of conduct.”

Bukabakwa was provisionally suspended after allegations of widespread sexual abuse in the DRC were made in the media in November 2022. He and five other coaches were provisionally suspended by Fecofa, including Donga Epapa Cédric who was sacked by his club, JMK, after allegedly asking a player to send him photos of his penis. No action was taken against him or any of the other coaches by Fecofa or Fifa following an investigation that cleared them all due to a lack of proven evidence. Cédric has previously denied the allegations.

Mosengo-Omba, who was elected as Fecofa’s president in May having stepped down as the Confederation of African Football’s general secretary two months earlier, promised to look into the previous cases once he has re-established a disciplinary committee. Fecofa had been under a Fifa-appointed normalisation committee from 2023 until his election.

“We will make sure that no one who is behaving like this will be involved in football in this country,” he said. “It’s an absolute priority for us. You cannot accept your country’s name being linked with this kind of behaviour.”

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 7: Coventry
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 18th (NB: this is not necessarily Ben Fisher’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st (Championship)

Prospects

“We are back”, as the banners proudly state. It is 25 years since, after relegation was confirmed, Match of the Day cameras lingered on a message held aloft by a Coventry City supporter named John Mullaney. “We’ll be back,” were the words he inked – in sky blue, of course – on a scrap of wallpaper. When Coventry celebrated returning to the top flight and lifted the Championship trophy in front of a capacity crowd, thousands of supporters held aloft new-look signs with a tweaked slogan to symbolise the journey coming full circle: “We are back”.

It has not been without pain along the way; nine years ago they were preparing for their first season in the fourth tier for 59 years, and from 2019 to 2021 they had to share St Andrew’s with the landlords Birmingham. That was not even their first spell of homelessness; in 2013-14, they played “home” games 35 miles away in Northampton. Many supporters will recall those harder times when Frank Lampard’s side kick off the new season in the Premier League curtain-raiser at champions Arsenal a week on Friday. Many will also remember the work of Mark Robins, who across two spells spent more than eight years in charge, en route to this point.

The biggest challenge will be adapting to the level. Lampard is a Premier League great but only seven of his squad count experience of the division on their CVs, the returning maverick Gus Hamer boasting the most starts among them (34) from his season in the top flight with Sheffield United. “Part of that is a good thing: we’re excited, hungry and the players want to show they deserve to be here,” Lampard said. “But we also have to work to help the squad to bridge the gap.”

Coventry’s recruitment has been superb under the sporting director, Dean Austin, and the club-record £23m arrival of Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi from the Danish side FC Nordsjælland is particularly exciting. Some of those who flourished upon joining in the second tier also look capable of stepping up, including Milan van Ewijk, Jack Rudoni and Carl Rushworth, who has signed permanently after a successful loan from Brighton. Goals were no problem last season: Coventry were the highest scorers in English football’s top four tiers with 97.

Aside from a playoff semi-final defeat to Sunderland last year and a bumpy start to this one, it has been largely smooth sailing since Lampard succeeded Robins in November 2024. Coventry lost seven league matches last season, only two at home, and the going will be tougher in the top tier. “We’ve won a lot of games at this club in the last year – it’s going to be much harder to do that in the Premier League,” Lampard said. “I’m not scared of that. We have to be excited by it.”

Off-field picture

Coventry launched a “storytelling space” at the club’s stadium to celebrate promotion and the path to this point. The first exhibition in the club’s museum is titled The Journey Back, which tells the club’s story from homelessness to the Premier League and showcases artefacts donated by supporters, players and managers and the owner, Doug King, opened last month. Promotion means abiding by Premier League regulations and the Coventry Building Society Arena, as it is now known, has dropped in capacity by about 300 seats in order to accommodate camera gantries and other changes to ensure compliance.

Owner-fan relationship

King angered supporters when sacking Robins but his decision was ultimately vindicated. King is never too proud to get involved: see him fist pumping the crowd, belting out the Enemy’s We’ll Live and Die in These Towns, the club’s de facto pre-match anthem, from the directors’ box, or swaying to Take That, who performed a trio of gigs at the stadium he bought 12 months ago – another big tick. Such is King’s popularity, supporters chant his name and a couple last season donned fancy dress to masquerade as him, wearing lanyards, sky-blue ties and bouffant wigs. “They tried to blag themselves into the boardroom ... but I’m way more handsome than them,” King said.

The manager

Promotion to the Premier League, Lampard says, marked the proudest moment of his managerial career. He went to work on his coaching badges after retiring and, 12 months after taking charge of Derby, he achieved his ultimate goal in double-quick time: managing Chelsea. A lot has happened since, including a stint “babysitting” the Blues when put in interim charge in April 2023. That seven-week period was his last exposure to the top flight as a manager but the familiar voices of his assistants Joe Edwards and Chris Jones remain. After 20 months in charge, he is comfortably the longest-serving of the three English managers in the division (Michael Carrick, eight months; Gary O’Neil, three months). Fresh from being named the League Managers Association manager of the year, an award presented to him by Thomas Tuchel, this summer Lampard signed fresh terms until 2029.

Star signing

Never fall in love with a loan player? Coventry did not just score goals last season, they kept them out, too, Rushworth claiming the Championship golden glove for 17 clean sheets. An ever-present in the league, his performances earned him three end-of-season club awards. On Coventry’s open-top bus parade, Rushworth, handed a pen by the captain, Matt Grimes, signed a placard that read “Sign here Carl” in block capitals. Then, this month, he signed a real contract to join permanently from Brighton, who inserted a buyback clause. “He was this close to getting kicked out of the group chat,” the defender Jake Bidwell joked after embracing Rushworth on his return. Before his season at Coventry, he had enjoyed loans across the league pyramid with Walsall, Lincoln, Swansea and Hull, but now the highly-regarded 25-year-old will test himself at the highest level.

View image in fullscreen Coventry valued Carl Rushworth so highly they spent a club-record £22.5m to sign him permanently from Brighton. Photograph: Richard Hammersley/Shutterstock

Stat attack

Arsenal were not the only champions to make good use of dead-ball situations last season. Coventry led the Championship for set-piece goals, with 29. Only Bayern Munich (0.65 goals per game) bettered their average (0.63) in the top divisions in England, France, Germany, Italy and Spain. The issue is whether they will win enough corners and free-kicks in the Premier League to exploit this ability.

Set for a breakthrough

Promotion makes the jump from the academy to the first team that little bit bigger but Kai Andrews has at least made a dent in the senior squad. The 20-year-old, who made his debut aged 17, made seven substitute appearances last season before being loaned to Hibernian. Competition has only got fiercer since but Andrews has plenty of admirers. “There’s just something more about this kid; he has a presence – and that excites me,” said Craig Bellamy, who played for Coventry at the beginning of his career and handed an 18-year-old Andrews a shock call-up to the Wales squad approaching 18 months ago.

World Cup impact

Did Yirenkyi have an inkling that he would soon call Brandon Thomas-Asante a clubmate after the striker set him up to score his first World Cup goal for Ghana? Thomas-Asante, one of five players to reach double figures for Coventry last season, made inroads down the left flank and then squared the ball to the six-yard box, where Yirenkyi was on hand to strike a 95th-minute winner against Panama in their opener in Toronto. Haji Wright, Coventry’s top scorer last season, made two late substitute appearances for the USA, while Aurèle Amenda was part of the Switzerland squad that reached the last 16 but did not play a minute.

Sports.title: ‘It was horrendous’: Durham captain relieved WSL2 club survived after fears of folding
Sports.content:
The Durham captain Sarah Wilson has spoken of her relief over the fresh investment that saved the club this summer, after what she recalled as a “horrendous” period worrying that the Women’s Super League 2 club could fold.

Durham finished 10th in England’s second tier last term and have been ever-present in WSL2 since 2014 but their ability to remain in the division was in major doubt when the club released a statement on 8 June warning that they would have to “cease operations” if they could not find fresh investment within 21 days. Later in June they were rescued when the local businessman and South Shields FC co-owner Geoff Thompson, together with his co-investor, agreed to acquire a majority stake in the club.

Wilson has played for Durham for 12 years and, recalling that mid-June period of uncertainty, she said: “There’s no way to sugarcoat it. It was horrendous. [For] a couple of weeks we didn’t know if we were coming or going or what was going on. And then all of a sudden we got the news that we had been saved and then within a couple of weeks we’ve got a new manager coming in so it’s just really exciting and it honestly feels now like nothing’s ever happened. It’s a breath of fresh air. It’s incredible.

“Going from a really difficult time to where we are now in such a short space of time is an absolute credit to the club. We all kind of found ourselves in a really difficult position, waitng for answers. I was trying to support the team as much as I could [as captain], just reassuring [teammates] and keeping in contact with everyone. And I must say, we were well looked after and information was shared when it could be shared. [But] it was just such an awful time. So when we found out the really good news, it was just like a huge weight lifted off our shoulders.

“There are so many jobs and young kids coming through that would have been massively affected and it would have been a massive shame for the north-east and for the club. Now it’s just really, really positive and really exciting to move forward with everything.”

Durham begin the new campaign at home to Southampton on 6 September, with what will be Durham’s new head coach Willie Kirk’s first match in charge, following his appointment in July.

It is the former Bristol City, Everton and Leicester manager’s first managerial job in English football since he was sacked by Leicester in March 2024. In the intervening years he has managed the Swedish sides Linköping and Djurgårdens IF.

Wilson has nothing but praise for the former Manchester United assistant manager, saying of Kirk: “[He’s been] brilliant, he’s just brought the club to a completely different new standard. When you’ve got someone who comes from that elite background, they bring all of those experiences.

“As soon as we found the news, it was like: ‘Right, OK, when do we start?’ He’s got some incredible experience working with some really top players. So he’s been fantastic.”

Sports.title: Failure not an option as Ange Postecoglou gears up for biggest challenge yet alongside Ronaldo | John Duerden
Sports.content:
When Ange Postecoglou left Nottingham Forest in October, few would have predicted his next port of call would be Riyadh, but taking over Al-Nassr is likely to be one of the biggest challenges of his varied career. This is a coach who always wins something in his second season but there is little chance of a second season if there is no trophy in the first. The fact that he is the club’s 12th coach in the 2020s alone is a stark reminder that failure is not an option, and the financial issues that have meant a quiet summer in the transfer market won’t be accepted as an excuse.

In May, Cristiano Ronaldo lifted the Saudi Pro League title and soon after Al-Nassr head coach Jorge Jesus, the septuagenarian who has won something in the first season of his last two Saudi spells, left to take the Portugal job. Taking over the Saudi Arabian champions and their star-studded squad may seem like a fairly comfortable gig but this will be anything but.

Expectations are higher than anywhere Postecoglou has been – that’s just the way it is for one of Saudi Arabia’s big four. Last season’s title was the first since 2019 and more of the same is demanded. But there is also a need for a first Asian Champions League title, a competition in which Postecoglou made little impact with Brisbane Roar and Yokohama F.Marinos. Even with the likes of Ronaldo, Sadio Mané and João Félix, a continental crown has remained elusive. Win one and Postecoglou will write his name into Al-Nassr’s history – as well as that of Asia, as the first coach to win the premier club and country titles – but it can’t come at the cost of finishing near the bottom of the league table, as happened at Tottenham. Challenging on two fronts is expected.

At Al-Nassr, three games without a win equals unrest. It is a club with plenty of former players ready to give opinions as often as television shows and websites want. Four games and it moves to another level. As a result, most coaches don’t worry too much about playing style and philosophy – winning is of utmost importance. There is little patience for a slow start while players get to grips with a new system, a new style or a new coach. There will be no waiting for a second season payoff. Al-Hilal won the King’s Cup last season, finished second in the league and were unbeaten. Many fans were still unhappy with Simone Inzaghi.

View image in fullscreen Postecoglou will team up with Cristiano Ronaldo at Al-Nassr. Photograph: Hamad I Mohammed/Reuters

And then there is Ronaldo. At 41, he is still the face of the league. Postecoglou has never managed a player even approaching such levels of fame and influence. Ronaldo doesn’t press or move around much these days, though he can still finish. The more than $6m-a-week man can be rested, especially in Asian Champions League group games, and it has been reported that he has been given extra time off after the World Cup and could miss Thursday’s opener against the newly-promoted Diriyah. He will, however, still expect to play the majority of matches – as does the league, club, media and fans. All are desperate for Ronaldo to reach the 1,000-goal milestone this season. He is just 24 short. It could become quite a sideshow.

There is not a huge amount of cover for the forward as Al-Nassr have not strengthened their squad since lifting the trophy, making more headlines for financial issues than transfer targets. At one point, it was reported that the club had debts of 800m Saudi Riyals, around A$300m, and were facing a transfer ban. The problem was cleared up by the Saudi Public Investment Fund – the owners of the club – along with a restructuring and commercial deals just days before kick-off. The departing Croatian Marcelo Brozović, a steady presence in midfield for three seasons, was replaced by Portugal’s Samú Costa last weekend, but if Postecoglou wants more, sales may need to be made. Meanwhile Al-Hilal, for example, spent a reported $130m on Crysencio Summerville.

Even if it does end quickly and in tears, the received wisdom in coaching circles is that losing your job in Saudi Arabia has little impact on employability back in Europe. Nuno Espírito Santo left Al-Ittihad after 16 months but smoothly returned to the Premier League and Nottingham Forest. In Postecoglou’s case, however, a third consecutive dismissal in a relatively short time won’t look good on his resume.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

At least Postecoglou will have a fellow Australian to chat to, with former Yokohama assistant and Newcastle Jets coach Arthur Papas now in charge of Al-Ettifaq. Al-Ettifaq have twice finished sixth and seventh in the past four seasons and it is clear what is regarded as success there – to break into the top five. That is far from easy given the resources of those that usually finish above them. Whether it is harder than Postecoglou’s challenge in the capital remains to be seen.

Sports.title: Atlético Madrid agree £34.1m deal for Tottenham’s Cristian Romero
Sports.content:
Tottenham have reached an agreement with Atlético Madrid over the sale of their captain, Cristian Romero. Romero was given the green light by the club and Roberto De Zerbi to depart Spurs this summer after a turbulent 2025-26 campaign in which he served four separate suspensions.

Inter initially led the chase for the Argentina centre-back, but after talks with Spurs stalled, long-term admirers Atlético swooped in and a package of €40m (£34.1m) is set to secure Diego Simeone his target.

It will bring a rollercoaster five-year spell in north London to an end for Romero, who joined in 2021 and enjoyed mixed success under Antonio Conte before a strong bond was formed with Ange Postecoglou.

Romero wore the captain’s armband when Tottenham ended a 17-year trophy drought with victory over Manchester United in the 2025 Europa League final and produced a fine performance to ensure Postecoglou’s promise of silverware in his second season came true.

However, Postecoglou’s dismissal weeks later was met with a thinly veiled social media post in the direction of Spurs’ hierarchy by Romero and more followed during a chaotic last season where only a final-day win against Everton avoided relegation.

Romero, who was made captain by Thomas Frank ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, was in Argentina days before Tottenham’s 1-0 success over Everton to receive treatment on a knee injury before he got a flight back to be present in the stands. The return of Romero for the relegation decider only occurred after widespread criticism from Spurs supporters and it proved the final nail in the coffin for many fans.

The World Cup winner will exit Spurs after 156 appearances and link up with his compatriot Simeone, who has repeatedly talked up the quality of the Argentinian in recent seasons and will finally get his man this summer.

Tottenham have inserted a 15% sell-on clause in the deal and this imminent departure continues a summer of mass changes with De Zerbi overseeing a huge revamp of a squad which has finished 17th in consecutive seasons.

Newly promoted Hull have broken their transfer record to sign the Senegal defender Nobel Mendy from Spanish side Rayo Vallecano. They also signed Australia international Lucas Herrington on Wednesday.

View image in fullscreen Lucas Herrington became Australia’s youngest player to make a World Cup appearance this summer. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Fifa/Getty Images

The Tigers have not disclosed the fee for the 21-year-old Mendy but it exceeds the reported £20m they paid for the Greece goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis last week. Mendy, who has one international cap and previously played for Paris FC and Real Betis, has signed a five-year deal, with an option for a further 12 months. He finished his only season with Rayo Vallecano with an appearance in May’s Conference League final loss to Crystal Palace.

“I have wanted to play in the Premier League since I was little, so it’s a great challenge to face and I am ready for it,” Mendy told Hull’s website.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Herrington, 18, became Australia’s youngest player to start a World Cup game for the Socceroos this summer, and arrived from MLS side Colorado Rapids on a five-year deal.

Crystal Palace have re-signed Aston Villa’s Evann Guessand on loan for the season with an option to buy. The Côte d’Ivoire international made 14 appearances after moving to Selhurst Park in January until the end of last season, but in July Palace opted against making the move permanent.

The 25-year-old joined Villa from Ligue 1 side Nice for £30m last summer but failed to win a regular place in Unai Emery’s side.

Celtic have signed the Egypt winger Haissem Hassan from Spanish club Real Oviedo, subject to international clearance. The 24-year-old, who impressed at this summer’s World Cup, joins the Scottish champions on a four-year deal, with the option of a further 12 months.

“When I heard about Celtic being interested in me, I had to get here and be part of the club,” Hassan told the club’s website. Manager Martin O’Neill said Celtic had done “really well” to secure a player of Hassan’s quality amid interest from other clubs.

“He is someone who I think has the ability and experience to do very well for us, performing at a high level in domestic and international football,” said O’Neill.

Sports.title: Transfer news LIVE: Chelsea set Fernandez deadline, Reijnders in talks over shock Saudi move, Romero agrees £34m Spurs exit
Sports.content:
Not backing down

Jamie O'Hara has refused to apologise for his previous comments about Brennan Johnson, despite Gabby Agbonlahor doing so.

The two talkSPORT pundits gave damning assessments of Johnson and Dwight McNeil's 2025/26 campaigns after the pair completed a swap deal - with McNeil moving to Selhurst Park, while Johnson headed to the Hill Dickinson.

Both Agbonlahor and O'Hara questioned the deal, with the latter saying: "It's like, 'We’ll give you crap, you give us crap back'."

This prompted Johnson himself to respond on Instagram, who said of the pair, 'Won more than both of these put together', which later prompted Agbonlahor to publicly apologise.

But O'Hara told talkSPORT Drive: “Being a footballer, you're going to take criticism. He obviously didn't like the fact that we said it was crap for crap.

“It was only a bit of a laugh but I get it. You get the hump with things. I've been called crap plenty of times. I get called crap every single day of the week.

“Don't take it personally. It is what it is, he has been crap.

“I'm not saying he's a bad player. Anyone who plays Premier League football, anyone who does what he's done, fair play. Brilliant.

“But last season Brennan Johnson was crap. He would be the first to admit it. Hopefully he goes to Everton and does all right.

“There's no apology needed. I know Gabby bottled it. Like he always does… he tried to throw me under the bus. Not the first time, won't be the last.

“But I'll stand by it. I think with Brennan Johnson he's got all the attributes to be a decent player. But he was crap [last season].”

Sports.title: Fulham forfeit trophy as opponents claim they abandoned match before its end
Sports.content:
Fulham forfeit trophy as opponents claim they abandoned match before its end

Fulham's pre-season clash against Malaga ended in bizarre fashion as the Spanish side conducted a penalty shootout on their own.

The contest at the Estadio La Rosaleda in Malaga finished 2-2 after 90 minutes, but with the Costa del Sol trophy on the line, there had to be a winner.



2 The two sides were set to contest a small piece of silverware Credit: Getty

However, no-one appeared to tell Fulham that was the case.

After the full-time whistle, Fulham's players shook hands and began to make their way off the pitch.

Meanwhile, Malaga forward Eneko Jauregi strode up to the penalty spot where he placed the ball and duly slotted home, albeit into an open goal.

Jauregi then jogged away to celebrate and gave a fist pump to the Malaga supporters before being mobbed by his teammates.



Fulham issue statement on not participating in penalty shootout

The puzzling post-match scenes prompted Fulham to issue a statement on social media to clarify the situation.

"Thank you for your excellent support in Malaga this evening," the statement read.



"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw."

There were reports Fulham chose not to participate in the penalty shootout because of a tight travel schedule, with the club due to fly back to London immediately after the match.



Whatever the reason, it mattered little to Malaga who took home the Costa del Sol trophy.

And they disputed Fulham's version of events in their own statement.

2 Arbeloa's evening didn't go as planned Credit: Getty

It read: "Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract.

"Malaga CF were therefore crowned champions of the XXXVI Costa del Sol Cervezas Victoria Cup."



The contest marked Fulham's penultimate pre-season friendly before the Premier League campaign gets underway on August 24.

How did Fulham v Malaga unfold?

Ryan Sessegnon put the Cottagers ahead before David Larrubia levelled the contest for the hosts.

Fulham striker Rodrigo Muniz nudged Fulham back in front, only for Jauregi to net a late equaliser from the spot.

There was still more controversy to come though as new Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa was sent off at full-time.



Arbeloa was handed his marching orders by referee Miguel Angel Ortiz Arias due to his furious protests over a decision.

The former Real Madrid boss' exit was met with boos and whistles from Malaga supporters, which only increased in volume when Fulham's players exited the field.

Arbeloa's side wrap up their pre-season preparations on August 15 against Stuttgart before beginning their domestic campaign on August 24 with a clash against Chelsea.
