World.title: Nick Reiner indicted on murder charges in parents' killings at their LA home
World.content:
Nick Reiner has been indicted on murder charges in the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, inside their Brentwood home last year.

On Wednesday, Nick Reiner pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder with the special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and murder by means of lying in wait, the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office said. He also faces a special allegation that he personally used a dangerous and deadly weapon, a knife.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20. The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.

CBS LA has reached out to Nick Reiner's public defender, Kimberly Greene, and a representative for the family.

Rob, 78, and Michele, 70, were found dead inside their Brentwood home on Dec. 14 by their daughter, Romy Reiner, according to multiple sources. The LA County Medical Examiner's Office said the couple died of "multiple sharp force injuries."

"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," District Attorney Nathan Hochman said. "The indictment unsealed today also adds a special circumstance allegation that the defendant committed the murders by means of lying in wait. We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."

The couple married in 1989 and had three children: sons Nick and Jake and daughter Romy.

Rob Reiner rose to fame for his role as Archie Bunker's son-in-law, Michael Stivic, better known as "Meathead" on CBS' "All in the Family." He won two Emmy Awards for the role.

He also made a name for himself in the film world, directing some of Hollywood's biggest movies such as "The Princess Bride," "When Harry Met Sally…," "A Few Good Men," "Stand by Me" and "This is Spinal Tap."

Michele Reiner was a successful photographer who took the photo of President Trump used on the cover of his book "The Art of the Deal," according to Variety.

The night before the killings, the Reiners attended a party at Conan O'Brien's, where Rob and Nick Reiner had a brief but loud argument, sources who were at the party told CBS News.

On the day the couple was found dead, they had plans with their longtime friends Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama, according to the former first lady.

If convicted on the charges, Nick Reiner faces death or life in state prison without the possibility of parole, the DA's Office said. The decision on whether the prosecutors will seek the death penalty will be made at a later date.

He remains in custody with no bail. His pretrial hearing is scheduled for Sept. 15.

The Associated Press contributed to his report.

World.title: With midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the U.S. heads toward the midterm elections, a gruelling primary season has further entrenched a rift between the insurgent progressive and centrist wings of the Democratic Party.

At stake is control of Congress this November and, beyond that, the presidency in 2028.

The centrists argue candidates touting moderate and pragmatic policies is the path to flipping seats from Republican control. While progressives say more uninspiring, establishment candidates will not galvanize a coalition of young people, the working class and diverse voters that could propel the party to victory.

"I don't even know how I could go about being sure which group has the most appeal," said Hans Noel, an associate professor of Government at Georgetown University and co-director of the Georgetown Democracy Initiative.

He says that while progressive candidates may alienate some voters who otherwise might have voted Democrat, they will also bring new voters to the party, including those who may not have voted at all.

There are also intangible characteristics, like personal likeability, said Noel: "How do you add that all up and make a strong prediction? It's hard."

LISTEN | What direction should the Democratic Party take?: Two Blocks from the White House 29:47 As progressives win U.S. primaries, what’s the direction of the Democratic Party?

Primary wins and losses

The primary season — where Democratic voters choose their candidates for upcoming general elections against Republicans — has given both sides wins, losses and lessons.

On Tuesday, in the key battleground state of Wisconsin progressives were dealt a blow when democratic voters narrowly chose moderate David Crowley in the primary for governor over self-described Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, who was projected to win in the polls.

Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley speaks to the media on Wednesday in Middleton, Wis., after winning the primary. Crowley will take on Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November's midterm election. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

Hong's campaign was plagued in its final days by past comments she made advocating for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and also saying it was time to "cancel Thanksgiving," calling it a celebration of colonialism. During the campaign, she backed away from all these comments, saying her views had evolved.

Hong ultimately wasn't endorsed by progressive flagbearers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Other races where moderates were able to hold progressive challengers at bay included those in Washington and Missouri .

In the swing state of Michigan earlier this month, however, progressive Addul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders, eked out a victory against centrist candidate Haley Stevens despite over $60 million being spent on her behalf, largely from super PACs.

WATCH | What Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory means for Democrats: Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory called a win for progressive Democrats | Duration 2:04 U.S. Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's narrow victory in a Michigan primary has been described as a win for progressive Democrats, but has some in the party worried that being seen as too progressive will hurt their chances to defeat Republicans in the upcoming midterms.

El-Sayed, like other progressive candidates, campaigned on issues like medicare for all, getting money out of politics, taxing billionaire wealth and calling for an end to military aid for Israel. He has also been praised for his communication skills.

In response to the U.S. President Donald Trump calling him "full of shit," El-Sayed shot back : "At least I don't let mine go all over the Oval Office."

El-Sayed's victory followed wins from progressive candidates who took on more moderate democrats in strongholds of New York and Colorado.

Notably, in Maine, another battleground state, progressive Graham Platner delivered a win before he dropped out due to sexual assault allegations.

Discontent among young voters

Bhaskar Sunkara, president of left-leaning magazine The Nation and former vice chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, says El-Sayed's win and others like it are a "huge check" on the Democratic Party.

"Voters, particularly young voters, are really discontent with the leadership of the party … and just generally feel that the Democratic Party doesn't stand for anything. It's not combative enough."

Progressive politicians U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, left, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, right, campaigned alongside Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed at July's the People V. The Powerful rally in Detroit. El-Sayed went on to win the Michigan senate primary nomination on Aug. 5, in a tight race. (Jose Juarez/The Associated Press)

Sunkara went on to say that El-Sayed is a better candidate than Hong with working-class voters.

"I think there is a way in which some candidates have been tarred with stances they had in 2019, 2020. This sort of abolish the police, the discussion of whiteness or whatever else. Abdul never had that problem."

Hong wasn't the only candidate backing off from past comments.

New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made headlines earlier this week when asked about her past support for defunding the police. "I have a local city councilman that has this saying: 'Woke 1 was crazy,' " she said before laughing.

Can progressives win key battleground states?

While some in the progressive wing re-evaluate past positions that could alienate voters this election cycle, many moderate democrats continue to warn of liabilities in swing states.

Fareed Zakaria, host of CNN's Sunday public affairs program GPS , cited Washington Post data to point out that while El-Sayed had the support of Michigan's most educated counties and college towns, his opponent did better in rural and lower-income areas.

"The left has the passion, but the middle still has the votes needed to win in general elections," Zakaria said.

Kate de Gruyter is the vice-president of communications at Third Way, a leading centrist democratic group that is spending $15 million between now and 2028 to discredit Democratic Socialism.

LISTEN | What's behind the wave of Democratic Socialist wins in the U.S.: Front Burner 36:53 Understanding the rise of ‘democratic socialism’

"Their theory of the case is that they're somehow going to be able to persuade all these voters in the middle that they absolutely need to win in November to back their candidate. We've never seen that happen over the entirety of the Trump era," she said in an interview.

De Gruyter added that El-Sayed's decision to campaign with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker as one example of "a whole universe of things that Republican ad makers are salivating at."

De Gruyter went on to suggest that the reason Democrat Kamala Harris lost the presidential election in 2024 was that she was seen as too lax on issues like immigration and plagued by stances she'd taken in the past on " transgender policy ."

In the final weeks of the campaign. Trump's team ran an ad using a five-year old clip of Harris saying that "every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access" to taxpayer-funded gender transitions.

"The idea that we should move further left makes no sense at all," she said.

The interesting thing is that while that can all be true, there are also plenty of arguments that suggest the opposite, according to Noel, the Georgetown associate professor.

U.S. Vice-President and then presidential candidate Kamala Harris takes part in a phone bank at the Democratic National Convention Headquarters on Nov. 5, 2024. Her unsuccessful campaign has been criticized by both progressives and moderate democrats. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

"And it can also be true that Harris actually lost because she was too tied to the establishment and Biden. And too close to Israel … progressives called her a cop. Either of those differences could have been enough because it was a fairly close race."

Either way, Democrats are riding favourable waves into the midterms.

Trump's polling is low . He has entered into an unpopular war in Iran . And all of this should help the Democrats, whether they're progressives or moderates in the mid-terms, said Noel, adding that if the Democrats don't do as well as expected there will be a lot of "what happened?"

"If all the progressive candidates lose and the centrist candidates win, well, that's going to be an easier story."

World.title: 'Exponential rise': Canadian pediatricians document severe e-scooter injuries, deaths in children, teens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As e-scooters become increasingly common across Canada, pediatricians, emergency physicians and other experts warn that injuries — often severe and involving younger people — are rising, while regulations struggle to keep pace.

Dr. Daniel Rosenfield, a pediatric emergency physician at SickKids hospital in Toronto and chair of the injury prevention committee for the Canadian Pediatric Society (CPS), says he has seen "a complete exponential rise" in every type of injury that can result from an e-scooter crash — from minor scrapes to major brain injuries and death.

Bad injuries used to be "once in a blue moon," he told CBC News. Now, "anytime we get a call from EMS that says, 'E-scooter trauma inbound,' we're prepared for severe injuries," he said.

E-scooter injury cases at SickKids rose from 26 in 2023 to 46 in 2024 and 107 in 2025, Rosenfield said.

"And this year we're likely on target for more than that."

The experience is mirrored across Canada and around the world. A CPS survey of Canadian pediatric specialists, conducted from late 2025 to early 2026 and published Thursday, documented 10 deaths, 12 ICU admissions and 26 hospitalizations lasting more than two days over the previous 12 months as a result of e-scooter crashes. Head injuries were present in about half the cases.

"The vast majority, if not all, are unhelmeted," Rosenfield said.

The most severe injuries tended to involve boys between 10 and 15 years old, he said.

The CPS survey records the experience of pediatric specialists rather than providing a rigorous quantitative analysis. But a separate study published Tuesday in the Emergency Medicine Journal provides multi-year hospital administrative data from three U.K. hospitals that closely aligns with what Canadian pediatricians are seeing.

That study found e-scooter cases at hospitals in Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield rose from fewer than 10 in 2019 to almost 150 in 2024. Head injuries were among the most severe, and fewer than two per cent of those injured were wearing helmets.

From 69 km/h to a critical care unit

That U.K. data mirrors what Canadian families are experiencing firsthand.

Just over a year ago in London, Ont., Crystal Dunkley's son Shaun was not wearing a helmet when he took a family friend's e-scooter out for a ride one evening, as he had done many times before.

That evening, Shaun, then 12, hit a raccoon as it ran across his path.

"He believes he was going 69 kilometres an hour when this happened," Crystal Dunkley recalled in a video interview Wednesday.

An ambulance rushed Shaun to the Children's Hospital in London, where he was intubated and admitted to the Pediatric Critical Care Unit with a fractured skull. He was in a coma for over a week.

"The doctors told us that with the brain bleed they determined he had, there was a possibility he would not make it, and if he did, then he would likely be very disabled," Crystal said.

Following his e-scooter crash, Shaun Dunkley was in a coma for over a week and spent more than a month in the London, Ont., children's hospital. (Crystal Dunkley)

Shaun ultimately recovered completely after 34 days in Children's Hospital and more time at a rehabilitation facility in Toronto. Crystal said he now approaches people riding e-scooters on the street and tells them to wear a helmet.

"Not a day goes by that I don't see multiple young children riding them without helmets, sometimes two or three to a scooter," Crystal said. "Some of these scooters can go … like I said, the one he was on was going 69 kilometres an hour."

'Anything but toys': Why regulation is lagging behind

Most parents are surprised by the extent of their child's injuries, Rosenfield said.

"And to be fair to the families, these devices are often marketed as toys," he said. "And as a device that can go zero to 40 kilometres an hour in a number of seconds, I will tell you they're anything but toys."

The CPS survey also notes that younger people may be less familiar with road rules, less risk-averse and at greater risk of injury because of their developmental stage.

But it also argues there are problems with rules and laws, describing them as "unclear and made up of a patchwork of regulations, varying depending on the province/territory."

The minimum age for riding an e-scooter varies by province, while some cities have banned the devices altogether — though those bans are often ignored. Several provinces, including B.C., Ontario and Quebec, cap e-scooter speeds at 24 or 25 kilometres per hour.

"I can tell you for sure people go faster than that," Rosenfield said.

Rosenfield is not advocating for an e-scooter ban, pointing to their utility to complement public transit and reduce automobile traffic.

"I do think they have a use in an urban environment," he said. "I just think we need to figure out what that looks like and how to make those devices safe."

World.title: Quebec man receives North America’s 1st transplant using regenerated liver technology
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 64-year-old Quebec man has become the first patient in North America to receive a regenerated liver thanks to a breakthrough technology that could make dozens of additional livers available for transplant in its first year alone.

Gérard Landry, a resident of Nouvelle on the south shore of Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula, spent about 15 years dealing with liver problems that eventually progressed to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Just before he was wheeled into surgery for a liver transplant, his doctor gave him some unexpected news about the organ: it was regenerated by a new machine, used for the first time at Montreal’s Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal, or CHUM.

“ [My doctor] told me about the new machine that he worked on for a few years,” Landry said. “It was like a Christmas gift."

The technology, called Liver Assist, allows doctors to treat and assess a donated liver outside the human body before transplanting it. For Landry, it meant receiving an organ that might otherwise have been considered too risky to use.

WATCH | A new liver thanks to new technology: This Quebec patient is the 1st in North America to receive a regenerated liver | Duration 1:51 Gérard Landry had been suffering from liver disease and cancer for 15 years. But now, he’s cancer-free thanks to a liver regenerated by a new machine – technology that could lead to more life-saving transplants.

Giving a donated liver a chance to recover

Dr. David Hénault, hepatopancreatobiliary surgeon and liver transplant specialist at the CHUM, led the project and performed Landry's operation.

He said the team had been preparing to use the technology for about three years.

The Liver Assist system works by connecting a donated liver to a machine that circulates an oxygen-rich fluid through the organ, which can help reverse some of the damage caused by a lack of oxygen while the organ is outside the body.

Dr. David Hénault, hepatopancreatobiliary surgeon and liver transplant specialist at the CHUM, led the project and performed the first operation in North America using the new technology. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

The technology then allows doctors to switch to a blood-based solution and assess how the liver functions in conditions designed to mimic the human body.

“If it works on the machine, then it’s going to work in the human,” Hénault said.

The liver Landry received was particularly well suited to the technology because it was susceptible to damage caused by a lack of oxygen during the organ transfer process, Hénault said.

Boost to number of available livers

The CHUM performs about 70 liver transplants each year. Hénault said a study done with Transplant Québec looked at livers that had previously been declined for transplantation and assessed which ones might have been recoverable using the new technology .

The team estimates the machine could make an additional 20 to 24 livers available for transplantation during its first year of use. That number could grow as the technology becomes more widely used.

“We will be able to help so many more patients in need of a liver that are waiting on the transplant list,” Hénault said.

Liver Assist is the new technology being used at Montreal’s CHUM and could make more donated livers available for transplant. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

He also says studies have shown the technology can help reduce complications, reoperations and hospital stay times for appropriate patients.

For Landry, doctors saw signs of a successful transplant almost immediately.

Hénault said Landry’s blood work the day after the operation was already better than expected for the type of transplant he received.

“I do believe that the machine really helped in this case,” Hénault said.

Landry’s recovery also appeared to be going unusually well.

“He was feeling way better than the average patient that gets a liver transplant,” Hénault said. “He did amazingly well.”

Looking forward to home

Landry is still recovering in Montreal and returns to the hospital for blood tests once or twice a week so doctors can adjust his medication.

Eventually, he hopes to return back east to Gaspésie and continue his recovery there. But after 15 years of illness, he's already thinking about what comes next.

“I’m in a hurry to see my family, my grandson, my friends and my horses,” he said.

Landry says he can't wait to go back home to his family and horses. (Submitted by Gérard Landry)

Landry also hopes his experience will encourage people to talk to their families about organ donation.

Even the most advanced technology cannot help, he said, if there are no donated organs available.

Because, as Landry put it, “if you have a horse without a rider, you don’t have a ride.”

World.title: She found an unidentified painting in storage. It turned out to be a female still-life master's work
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Hiding in plain sight, Clara Peeters painting discovered in a museum's storage: As It Happens 6:42 Hiding in plain sight: A lost masterpiece by an overlooked female artist discovered in a museum's storage

When art historian and curator Cynthia Osiecki stumbled upon an unattributed still-life painting in an Oslo museum storeroom in 2022, she couldn't shake the feeling that she knew exactly who created it.

"We were trying to buy a work by Clara Peeters, like many museums are trying to purchase women artists at the moment,” said Osiecki, who had been studying the work of the pioneering 17th-century Flemish Baroque artist.

When she spotted the painting, Osiecki wondered if it could be a long-lost work by Peeters.

“I mean, it’s almost too good to be true to have a Clara Peeters hanging right in your storage while the museum was actively looking for women artists on the art market,” Osiecki said. “Instead of having to purchase one, we might have had one all this time and right under our nose and didn’t even know it.”

Despite her groundbreaking work, the enigmatic artist remains relatively unknown to the wider public, a fate shared by many female artists of her time, Osiecki says.

That's part of the reason why the National Museum of Norway is putting a spotlight on historic female artists, with Woman Painter opening in Oslo on Oct. 8. The show will feature works by 19 female artists who worked across northern Europe and Italy between 1550 and 1650, including Judith Leyster, Lavinia Fontana, Artemisia Gentileschi, and, of course, Peeters.

Painstaking work to attribute painting

The piece Osiecki discovered, titled Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza, had once been believed to be the work of Ambrosius Brueghel, a member of a famous family of artists in Antwerp, Belgium. It was later reclassified as "anonymous" and sent to storage.

Earlier this year, however, it was officially reattributed to Peeters, a painstaking journey spanning several years, Osiecki says.

A journey that wouldn't have begun if not for her keen eye.

When she first discovered painting, Osiecki found some telltale clues.

Another piece by Clara Peeters, created in 1621, called Still Life with fish, a candle, artichokes, crab and prawns that hangs in the Prado. (Museo del Prado)

Along with being one of the earliest specialists of still-life painting of her era, Peeters was known for embedding her own likeness into everyday objects in her works. She did this by painting tiny self-portraits in the shiny surfaces of pewter jugs, fruits or vegetables — subtly claiming ownership and asserting her own professional identity in a male-dominated world, Osiecki says.

The Oslo painting features nine dead birds — considered a delicacy in the 17th-century, Osiecki says — freshly-picked hazelnuts and apricots.

The grapes, in particular, stood out to Osiecki.

“In our grapes, there is a reflection of a person, but it’s not in any way as detailed as those silhouettes are on other paintings by [Peeters'] hand,” said Osiecki.

Then there were other details that caught her eye — the tazza, a saucer-like drinking vessel from the period that Peeters frequently featured in her paintings — as well as the distinctive positioning of the birds within the composition, Osiecki says.

WATCH | Why he’s scouring the art world for his great-great-grandfather’s lost paintings: Why he’s scouring the art world for his great-great-grandfather’s lost paintings | Duration 5:06 Jonathan Wener has spent half a century searching for his great-great-grandfather William Raphael’s lost artworks. The 19th-century Montreal artist made paintings depicting life in Quebec during that time, but Wener says his ancestor didn’t get the recognition he deserved.

“I also knew that many of her contemporaries were using the same objects in Antwerp [Belgium] at the time,” she said. “So I had to tread very, very carefully to make sure it really was Clara Peeters and not me wanting it to be Clara Peeters.”

There was also another hitch: woodworms had eaten away at the bottom edge of the painting where Peeters would have typically signed her name.

Despite this, Osiecki remained determined to ferret out the true artist behind the piece. She and her colleagues spent several years studying and comparing other works by Peeters and her contemporaries, she says. The museum's conservator cleaned the Oslo piece and took better pictures, she adds. Slowly, but steadily, the process confirmed the attribution: Peeters was the painter.

Now the painting is set to take centre stage at the Oct. 8 show.

Nora Ceciliedatter, director of collections and exhibitions and the National Museum of Norway, says the Woman Painter exhibition is part of a "broader effort to bring visibility to artistic careers and perspectives that have been historically underrepresented at the museum."

For Osiecki, the painting's long journey back to Peeters' name demonstrates how much work remains to be done to uncover female artists whose contributions have been overlooked, misattributed or simply forgotten.

“We have to continue doing this because there are so many paintings out there that are either anonymous or attributed to male artists,” she said. “The more research we do to women artists, the more works we find by them, and this is really time and effort well-spent.”

World.title: Woman behind petition to oust U.S ambassador says response is 'beyond what I expected'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The woman behind a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country says it's grown beyond her expectations.

The online petition, which is set to be presented in the House of Commons in the fall, says Pete Hoekstra should be declared persona non grata and the Canadian government should request his removal as U.S. ambassador to Canada.

More than 70,000 people had signed the petition as of Wednesday evening, approximately double the number of signatures 24 hours earlier.

"It's beyond what I expected out of this," said Lee Walker, the Calgary-based woman behind the petition, in an email to CBC News.

"It tells me that it's not a fringe issue, and that a lot of Canadians are uncomfortable with how Hoekstra has been repeating Trump talking points about our sovereignty and Canada as a whole."

Walker's petition accuses Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship and of "making repeated interventions in Canadian political discourse inconsistent with diplomatic protocol."

The petition also says Hoekstra has normalized the Trump administration's threats to annex Canada. The ambassador made headlines in June after saying that Canada's annexation by the United States would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Walker said comments like that from an ambassador aren't appropriate.

"Words from someone in his position carry immense weight, and normalizing that kind of rhetoric can have real consequences," she said.

Hoekstra has also said it's dangerous for Canadian political leaders to describe the Trump administration's ongoing tariff campaign as a trade war and has criticized Canadian politicians who have responded to the tariffs by discouraging travel to the U.S. and for pulling American liquor off of shelves.

'Turmoil already exists'

The petition also calls on the Liberal government to direct a parliamentary committee to review U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian affairs.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa declined to comment on the petition except to say the embassy is aware of it.

When asked about the potential impact the petition could have amid sensitive trade talks between the U.S. and Canada, Walker said there's already tension between the two countries.

"The turmoil already exists. It's just one-sided right now," she said.

Walker said her intention is to make clear " that respect for Canada and its sovereignty isn't optional or up for negotiation."

Canadian and American negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

WATCH | More about the petition: Canadian petition calls to expel U.S. ambassador | Duration 0:34 Nearly 30,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country. The online petition accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

The petition will be presented in Parliament by Green Party Leader Elizabeth May in the fall. Members of Parliament can table petitions in the House of Commons without endorsing their contents.

As for what she wants to happen once it's presented, Walker said she's not sure the government will take steps to declare Hoekstra persona non grata, but hopes the petition will send a message.

"This sort of conduct from a sitting ambassador isn't something we'll just shrug off," she said.

World.title: Babies and toddlers are sweltering in some daycares. Should there be mandatory AC?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the hottest days last summer, Lyndsay MacKay would arrive at her 16-month-old son's daycare to find him in a diaper, his skin sticky and his hair plastered to his head.

He would collapse in her arms. Some nights, he'd fall asleep at the dinner table.

She said she knew the educators were doing what they could: ice cubes in the water tables, offering popsicles, darkening the rooms and placing cool cloths on the infants and toddlers.

"But at the end of the day, they're still hot, they're sweaty, they're exhausted," said the Toronto mother and early childhood education professor at Humber Polytechnic.

"From a health and safety and from a development perspective, the children are not — the children are almost just surviving the day."

MacKay is among the growing number of parents, educators, health and legal advocates across Canada lobbying for maximum indoor temperature at daycares, likely 26 C, akin to standards adopted for long-term care facilities in Ontario .

Like seniors, infants, toddlers and preschool-aged children are at a higher risk of developing heat exhaustion and its more severe form, heatstroke.

In part, it's because they have a higher metabolism than adults, creating more heat in their bodies. And, since their sweat glands are less efficient, it's harder to cool down. Plus, babies and young toddlers can't tell caregivers they're overheated.

What to watch for

Even preschoolers likely can't recognize what's happening, said Dr. Kirstin Weerdenburg, a pediatrician in the emergency department at Halifax's IWK Health Centre.

"They don't have a way to explain how they're feeling, so it's [about] knowing their behaviours and all those other physical signs and symptoms," she said.

"If someone's not paying attention to that, they might get, you know, looked over until you get to the more extremes."

At Tree of Life Nature Play School in Victoria, B.C., children head to the ocean to try to stay cool on the hottest days. (Submitted by Kate Lawes)

In young children, Weerdenburg said, symptoms can look like fatigue, flushed skin, irritability — even having trouble walking, which is a sign of dizziness.

But heat illness presents on a spectrum, so if kids are acting out of character on a hot day, she said it's worth paying attention.

Kids can often be treated at home with fluids and a cool room. But extreme cases of dehydration can make babies or young children too tired to drink, so they require IV fluids, the pediatrician said.

In the most severe cases, organs like the liver and kidney can shut down as the body redirects blood to the skin to help cool it. The heart speeds up, causing an arrhythmia, as it tries to pump more blood faster.

Keeping watch in the heat

Watching for signs of heatstroke is stressful for educators, said Amy O'Neil, executive director of Toronto's Treetop Children's Centre, noting they're not health-care professionals and don't have the training to make a diagnosis.

It's why she introduced air-conditioning at her child-care centre in 2019, and why she thinks the provincial and federal governments should also consider high temperatures in daycares to be unacceptable.

It's not a "comfort issue" but a matter of safety, said O'Neil, who is also board chair of Toronto Community for Better Child Care, an advocacy group of parents and educators for well-funded, publicly available child care.

"It's really hard to understand why the legislation — and in Ontario, it's the Child Care and Early Years Act — is so clear about maintaining minimum indoor temperatures in the winter, yet it's completely silent on maximum indoor temperatures during extreme heat."

WATCH | Expect more hot days to come: Why summer weather is hotter, arriving earlier and lasting longer | Duration 6:18 New research from the University of B.C. suggests summers are quickly stretching further into the spring and fall. To explain what this means for the Lower Mainland, CBC’s Michelle Eliot spoke with the lead researcher of the study, Ted Scott, who said the change will lead to extreme heat and more forest fires.

It cost upwards of $40,000, between $5,000 and $7,000 for each unit, to install eight air conditioners in June 2019, O'Neil said, paid for from the centre's reserve fund.

"It's a lot of money for a non-profit community-based child-care centre to swallow."

Premier Doug Ford pictured June 2, said last summer that he would 'look at' maximum indoor daycare temperature, but lobbyists say they have seen no movement. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Ontario Premier Doug Ford did say last summer that he would "look at" maximum indoor temperatures in daycare.

"I can't answer if we're putting 'em into standards," he told The Trillium in August 2025 in response to a question about temperature regulations. "We did that with the long-term care, now they all have air conditioning, and so we'll look at it with the kids as well."

It doesn't appear there has been any movement on the issue.

In response to an email to Ford's office asking about an update this week, the education minister's office instead provided a statement.

"Licensed child-care operators are responsible for providing a safe environment for the children in their care, including taking appropriate steps to protect them during periods of extreme heat," said part of the statement from Minister Paul Calandra's office.

What the regulations say

Other provinces have similarly vague regulations. None have instituted maximum indoor temperatures, though some regions require a heat source in the winter.

In B.C., regulations under the Community Care and Assisted Living Act require only that licensed daycares "provide a healthy and safe environment and maintain emergency response procedures," according to a statement from the province's Ministry of Health.

While the regulations do "not establish a specific indoor temperature limit," the statement notes that provincial health authorities have guidelines recommending the 26 C threshold, though these are not enshrined in law.

In Nova Scotia, a campaign recently launched by the parent advocacy group For Our Kids to regulate temperatures in schools, where many daycares operate year-round. Though the province's Early Learning and Child Care Regulations includes detailed guidelines about other essentials — providing developmentally appropriate toys, utensils and a safe place and opportunity for sleep — there is nothing about maintaining safe temperatures.

It's unclear, too, how many daycares across Canada have air-conditioning.

Getting that data and monitoring exactly how hot daycare classrooms are getting is critical, according to Jacqueline Wilson of the Canadian Environmental Law Association. CELA has been calling both for maximum indoor temperature legislation and funding for retrofitting, noting that Ontario was able to do that for the long-term care industry in 2021.

The observed annual global average temperatures for each year from 1980 to 2025 are shown relative to the pre-industrial global mean temperature. (Climate Data Canada)

While there's significant research showing that a maximum temperature of 26 C is appropriate for older adults, children's bodies may require an even lower threshold, Wilson said.

In its 2025 report on daycare temperatures, CELA suggests the exact temperature should be revisited every two years as more evidence becomes available and summers get hotter. Indeed, Environment and Climate Change released a forecast earlier this year suggesting that 2026 to 2030 is expected to be the warmest five-year period ever recorded.

More wildfires, too

Wildfires are increasing alongside summer temperatures, something Kate Lawes contended with when at her daycare, Tree of Life Nature Play School in Victoria.

She jokingly recalls how her public health authority used to issue "slip, slap, slop" heat advisory notices. Now, they focus on extreme temperatures, wildfires and air quality.

On the warmest days, she used to plan outings by the ocean or the forest — where the temperature would often be five to 10 degrees cooler. But the wildfires and accompanying air quality warnings make that impossible, the daycare manager said, as does opening the windows to allow cooler air inside in the early morning.

"We err on the side of caution," she said. "Their lungs are still growing and developing."

Her daycare kids used to take refuge from the heat by the ocean, now, they have to carefully plan those days because of wildfire smoke, Kate Lawes said. (Submitted by Kate Lawes)

She closed her school during the heat dome in 2021 that killed 619 people in B.C. and led to a maximum heat bylaw enacted in New Westminster, B.C., this summer for tenancy buildings.

It also prompted her daycare to buy a heat pump, an electric device that provides cooling in summer and heat in winter, which wasn't covered by the province's emergency preparedness fund.

Now the children and staff feel comfortable, she said, and it's lifted the stress that kids might become sick from the heat.

In Toronto, MacKay is thankful her son's daycare now has air-conditioning.

"He has energy," she said. "He's bright. He's not a wet noodle — he is a live wire."

World.title: 4 ex-Western University students accused in London, Ont., explosives-making scheme face 19 new charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The four people accused in a London, Ont., explosives and firearms-manufacturing investigation now face 19 new charges, according to court documents filed Tuesday.

Jerry Tong, Zekun (Alex) Wang, Fei (Frank) Han and Feiyang (Astrid) Ji were charged in January. All four were students or recent graduates of Western University, with the three men having studied in the engineering department.

The amended list of charges filed with the Ontario Court of Justice brings the total to 31 separate counts. Some of the charges are joint counts against all four, while others pertain to the specific accused.

The newest charges include possession of five specific explosive substances, possession of stolen property and access to computer data related to making firearms.

The lengthy investigation dates back to Jan. 24, when police responded to an overnight trespassing call at Western after two men entered one of the school's engineering buildings.

One person was arrested just outside the building. An investigation led police to a house in the nearby University Heights neighbourhood, where the other three were taken into custody.

Police spent days investigating inside the residence at 212 Chesham Place in London. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

Police completed a multi-day search of the residence at 212 Chesham Place, where Wang, Han and Ji lived, as well as two additional homes in Orléans, in suburban Ottawa, and Gatineau, Que.

Firearms charges in other cities

When they were first arrested, the four faced multiple firearms charges, including the manufacturing of a handgun and possession of a loaded restricted handgun.

New charges against Tong, Wang and Ji include the possession of magazines and suppression devices, as well as possession of another prohibited firearm. Tong and Wang are also now accused of handing and carelessly storing a rifle.

Tong, who faces the majority of charges, also has new counts related to events in other cities. He's been charged with storing rifles at a home in Orleans, manufacturing a prohibited firearm in Ottawa and possessing a rifle at an unauthorized location in Quebec.

Court documents show that Tong held a firearms licence, but some of his charges relate to possessing a firearm at a place not indicated on his licence.

WATCH | How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe: How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe | Duration 2:14 Four people are in custody after police discovered chemicals they say could be used to create explosives at a home in London, Ont. But, new information shows the suspects were working on developing an anti-drone weapon system. Here’s what we know so far.

Tong and Wang also face new charges related to events that happened months before they were arrested.

Wang is now charged with manufacturing a weapon between Sept. 1, 2025, and Jan. 24, 2026, while the pair are charged with breaking into a Western building on Oct. 9, 2025.

Explosive substances revealed

Court documents also show that Tong, Wang, Han and Ji face a new list of charges for possessing explosive substances, and names them for the first time.

They are accused of possessing pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN), trinitrotoluene (TNT), dinitrophenol (DNP), hexamethylene triperoxide diamine (HMTD) and lead azide.

Originally, all four were charged with possession of precursor substances and finished high explosives.

London police are seen outside the home at 212 Chesham Place on Feb. 2. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

All four also face a new count of possessing property of Western University valued at less than $5,000.

Wang faces a solo charge of accessing computer data that pertains to a firearm or a prohibited device, specifically, design files capable of being used with a 3D printer, metal milling machine or similar computer system for the purpose of manufacturing a device.

2 out on bail, 2 in custody

In total, these are the number of charges each accused faces:

Tong: 28.

Wang: 20.

Han: 11.

Ji: 13.

The four are still making their way through the courts, with two out on bail and two still in custody.

Tong did not request bail and remains in custody. Han was denied bail and remanded back into custody in February.

Wang was granted bail in March under strict conditions, including 24-hour house arrest and constant supervision from two sureties, who each posted $200,000. Ji is also out on bail with no sureties.

World.title: Canada, U.S. not yet ready to make tariff deal, Canada unsatisfied with latest U.S. offer: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the clock ticks toward U.S. President Donald Trump's latest tariff deadline, Canada and the U.S. aren't at a point where a tariff deal can be reached — and Canadian officials are not satisfied with the latest U.S. offer, according to two sources with knowledge of the trade talks.

According to sources on both sides of the border, the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see. CBC News is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

The Americans are seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and cover security and energy, the sources said.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

Sources told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Both sides have agreed to hold daily meetings at various levels up until that deadline, the sources said.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

Neither LeBlanc nor Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, answered reporters' questions after they were seen leaving Greer's office on Tuesday afternoon.

LeBlanc later posted to X saying that discussions are "ongoing" and he and Charette will "continue to engage at the negotiation table."

LeBlanc's office told CBC News he and Charette remain in Washington as of Wednesday night.

In addition to trying to dissuade Americans from levying new tariffs, LeBlanc and Charette are looking for relief on tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber and autos.

Canada is also hoping the ongoing trade talks between the two countries will result in a renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) after the Trump administration last month declined to extend the deal past 2036.

WATCH | Canada not satisfied with latest U.S. trade offer, sources say: Canada rejects latest U.S. trade offer days before tariff deadline | Duration 1:48 One week before new 50 per cent tariffs on billions in Canadian goods are set to kick in, Canada has rejected the latest U.S. counter-offer on a trade deal, sources tell CBC News.

When announcing the Aug. 19 tariffs, the U.S. raised a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged Canadian discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Carney on Sunday, calling on him to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up.

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving," Poilievre wrote.

Industry sources previously told CBC News that Canada is preparing to meet some U.S. demands — including ending the booze bans — in exchange for tariff relief.
