World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Quick hits: A 'peanut' jibe, a Starc record and a brain explosion
World.content:
Steve Smith called a Bangladesh bowler a "peanut" for making an appeal, but he could probably have labelled a couple of his batting colleagues as such on a dire batting display for Australia.

Meanwhile, Mitch Starc collected another accolade with yet another top order wicket for the Aussies

As it happened: Bangladesh minnows humble Australia's giants on day one in Darwin

Here are the quick hits from day one of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Weatherald falls in front of hometown crowd

Weatherald was unable to impress in front of his home crowd. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Local boy Jake Weatherald began the first Test under significant pressure, having clung onto his opening spot after struggling through his debut series against England.

And there was significant support for the Northern Territorian in Darwin, with the crowd rising and falling as he attempted to get his innings going.

But once again, Weatherald was unable to find his feet at Test level, eventually reaching and swiping and nicking off for an unconvincing 23 off 37 deliveries.

It was Weatherald's 10th sub-50 score from his 11 Test innings, and one that only raised more questions about his viability as a Test match opener

Weatherald, the first Australian men's Test cricketer born and raised in the Northern Territory and now the first Territorian to play Test cricket in Darwin, with three more opportunities to secure a spot on the plane to South Africa in October.

2. Green's pre-lunch brain explosion

Bangladesh was overjoyed to claim Green's wicket with the final ball before lunch. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With Australia teetering at 3-61, the under-pressure Cam Green decided to take the game on.

Perhaps the Australian most in need of a score, the all-rounder began his innings with a pair of well-timed drives, before hooking Taskin Ahmed for a maximum over backward square leg.

However, Green's counterattack was short lived, with the big man playing one shot too many in the shadows of the first break.

With what turned out to be the final ball of the morning session, Green all but gave his wicket away, meekly chipping one to a grateful Mushfiqur Rahim on the on-side.

Australia headed to lunch at 4-74, Bangladesh couldn't believe their luck, and Green, having come out with such purpose, trudged off for a run-a-ball 13.

3. Smith's triple reprieve

So often the man for a crisis, Steve Smith is no stranger to standing tall as wickets tumble around him.

But Australia's idiosyncratic world beater was anything but convincing as he somehow managed to prod his way to lunch after coming to the crease at 2-52.

Smith should have been out on 2, with his thick edge falling through the fingers of a stooping second slip.

A matter of balls later, Smith was once again nicking towards the cordon — but this time, the ball flew through a gap between second slip and gully, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto having only just removed a man from behind the wicket.

And it appeared that Smith's luck was well and truly in when he survived a line-ball DRS review.

With Smith swinging hard outside off, Bangladesh went up for caught behind with some confidence. Umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved, and Shanto wasted no time in sending the decision upstairs.

The technology, however, showed no conclusive evidence of an edge, with the ball passing perilously close to Smith's blade but failing to make its mark on ultra edge.

Bangladesh couldn't believe it as Smith was handed his third reprieve of the morning.

4. Smith talks Bangladesh out of a review, lands "peanut" jibe

Smith talked Bangladesh out of a review before late in the second session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having burnt two reviews in the first session, Bangladesh had just one DRS Hail Mary to play with for the bulk of the Australian innings.

Late in the second session, seamer Ebadot Hussein was tempted to break the glass for one that he never should have been.

His LBW shout against Smith was clearly far too high, but that didn't stop the Bangladeshi brains trust gathering for a serious discussion in the middle.

Smith couldn't believe it.

"Knee roll you reckon? It was up here you peanut!" Smith could be heard saying through the stump mic, gesturing to his hip area.

"What game are you watching?"

Smith's derision was enough to talk Bangladesh out of the review, but his honesty didn't end up counting for much — the Australian vice-captain eventually top-edging a short ball to be caught for 71.

5. Starc makes history

DARWIN, AUSTRALIA - AUGUST 13: Mitchell Starc of Australia celebrates with team mates after dismissing Shadman Islam of Bangladesh during day one of the First Test Match in the series between Australia and Bangladesh at Marrara Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Darwin, Australia. (Photo by Albert Perez - CA/Cricket Australia via Getty Images) (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

The records keep coming for Australia's top-order destroyer, Mitchell Starc.

Fresh from being named his country's Test player of the year last Friday, the 36-year-old carved out another piece of history, becoming the most lethal left arm bowler in the history of the format.

Starc procured a leading edge from opener Shadman Islam to claim the 434th wicket of his Test career, with Nathan Lyon making amends for an earlier dropped chance.

Starc's milestone scalp took him past former Sri Lanka spinner Rangana Herath.

However, that was the only breakthrough of the day in what was a humbling start to the season for Australia.

World.title: Man found guilty of killing his cousin after drug disagreement
World.content:
A judge has found a man who stabbed his cousin multiple times on the New South Wales Mid North Coast in 2023 not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter.

Conrad Lardner, 51, was arrested on May 17, 2023, and charged with murdering his 39-year-old cousin David Vale.

Mr Vale was found with stab wounds on Robert Eggins Street in South Kempsey on March 1, 2023.

The judge-alone murder trial began on June 29 at Port Macquarie Supreme Court and ran for four weeks.

The court heard Lardner stabbed Mr Vale twice, with one puncture to the lower side of the chest and another through his rib cage and heart.

Mr Vale died within 15 minutes.

Judge Campbell delivered his verdict today, accepting that Lardner killed Mr Vale but saying there was insufficient evidence to prove intent.

"I accept it is possible he armed himself with the knife, but there is no real evidence that supports the possibility, other than having the opportunity to do so," he said.

Fight over bad drugs

The families of Conrad Lardner outside Port Macquarie Courthouse. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

During Lardner's cross-examination, he told the court Mr Vale confronted him complaining about the quality of the drugs he was sold.

"I want my f****** money back, what you gave me was shit I went to sleep on it," Lardner told the trial.

"I said, 'There's not a refund,'" Lardner told the court.

Conrad Lardner was found guilty of manslaughter in the judge-alone trial. (Supplied: Facebook)

Justice Stephen Campbell told the court he did not accept the defence's evidence that Mr Vale bought drugs from Lardner on the morning of the stabbing.

"The accused gave evidence when the deceased arrived he was raving on about drugs the accused sold him," Justice Campbell said.

"I do not accept what the accused said happened on the morning or that he never supplied drugs to the deceased ever.

"It seems to follow when the deceased complained about good quality drugs he was referring to a previous supply at some earlier point in time that evidence does not disclose."

It was the Crown case that during the "scuffle" between Mr Vale and Lardner outside the home, Lardner went back into the kitchen and retrieved a knife before stabbing Mr Vale twice.

Justice Campbell said he was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt Lardner's "voluntary act" caused Mr Vale's death.

"The fact the accused stabbed twice with a knife provides some evidence of intent to inflict serious grievous bodily harm," he said.

Defence barrister Dennis Stewart said Lardner acted in self-defence and that he picked up the knife which fell out of Mr Vale's pocket.

Conflicting accounts

Judge Campbell told the court that the 20 witnesses who gave evidence during the trial, including Lardner, were "contradicted, discredited and challenged" by prior statements made to police or witnesses.

"I am satisfied to a necessary degree the deceased had developed a grievance over the accused over the supply of inferior quality drugs which did not give him the desire he wanted," Justice Campbell said.

"It just seems preposterous the deceased would bail him up about defective drugs which had never been supplied by him."

Jessica Howard said her family was glad Lardner was found guilty of manslaughter (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

Jessica Howard, who was David Vale's partner at the time, said she was glad he "got some justice".

"I'm glad the outcome was manslaughter and not not guilty," Ms Howard said.

"I don't really know how I feel because nothing is going to bring David back."

" It affects us everyday, he was a good father and we no longer have him with us anymore. "

Lardner was originally refused bail but he was released on conditional bail on November 11, 2023.

Today, Justice Campbell refused him bail to be sentenced on November 13.

World.title: Family breaks silence after man accused of running over kids gets bail
World.content:
A family member of an Aboriginal boy who was seriously injured when he was struck by a ute last week has spoken for the first time, expressing "deep concern and disappointment" after the accused driver was granted bail yesterday.

This article contains offensive language.

The incident occurred last Thursday night in the heart of Mildura, when two 12-year-old boys riding motorised bicycles through Langtree Mall were allegedly pursued and struck by a ute travelling at almost 80 kilometres per hour.

A family member of one of the boys has provided a statement to the ABC.

"I witnessed firsthand the physical and emotional impact this incident has had," they wrote in a statement.

"I sat beside my young cousin at Mildura Base Hospital while he was in pain and frightened. My cousin told us that he did not understand why the man was allegedly chasing them.

"The boys were scared, and their families have been left dealing with the emotional consequences of what occurred."

One of the boys was airlifted to the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne. The other was treated at Mildura Base Hospital. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

One of the boys suffered a collapsed lung and required surgery after suffering a broken arm, leg, ankle, sternum and multiple rib fractures. The other was concussed and had minor arm injuries.

There has been speculation that the two boys were earlier involved in an incident in the mall but in court on Wednesday Senior Constable Mitchell Carew confirmed the two boys were "categorically" not involved in any offences.

The boys were riding motorised pushbike in a mall. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

In a statement, Victoria Police asked the community not to spread false information.

"We remind the community to avoid sharing misinformation and rumours online, particularly while legal proceedings are underway," a spokesperson said.

On Wednesday Andrew Brien, 56, faced Mildura Magistrates' Court charged with four counts of reckless conduct endangering life, as well as counts of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing injury, and driving in a dangerous manner.

Andrew Brien was granted bail this week. (Facebook)

During the bail hearing a series of CCTV footage was shown.

In the first video, the vehicle allegedly driven by Mr Brien appears to have narrowly missed the two boys, carried out a U-turn and allegedly followed them into Langtree Mall.

The footage then showed the vehicle crashing into a bike at high speed, sending one boy flying through the air, before the ute collided with a streetlight pole.

The footage also showed one of the boys stuck underneath the ute and Mr Brien stepping over them without rendering assistance. The court heard call logs showed Mr Brien had called Triple Zero (000).

Mr Brien's lawyer argued his client was suitable for bail because he had no prior convictions, had spent his first time in custody, and a trial would likely not occur until 2028.

That was opposed by prosecutor Raphael de Vietri, who argued Mr Brien was motivated by a mistaken belief the boys had vandalised his partner's business, alleging that he was "deadset on mowing those two children down".

One of the boys suffered a collapsed lung and required surgery. The second child was concussed and had minor arm injuries. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

The court granted Mr Brien bail, noting he had never previously been in trouble and was not a suspected flight risk.

The court noted that it was largely influenced by the prospect of a lengthy delay in the court matter.

Mr Brien has been granted bail under the provision that he not drive a car and must adhere to a 9pm curfew. He will appear in court again in December.

Social media flooded with racist, violent comments

Days after the incident, racist and violent commentary spread across social media with false accusations that the children had committed a crime, something the family says has compounded their trauma.

Comments made on social media in the days after the news broke of the incident. (ABC News Graphics)

"As an Aboriginal family, seeing racist and hateful comments surrounding an already distressing situation added another layer of hurt," the family member said in their statement.

"The subsequent removal of posts does not erase the impact those comments had on the families who saw them.

"This raises broader questions for me about whether victims and their families — particularly Aboriginal children and families — feel adequately protected, supported and heard throughout the justice process."

Calls to review bail laws

During an interview with Channel 7 News local MP Jade Benham commented on the incident earlier this week, linking it to concerns about the crime rates in the area.

"This is not the way to go about it," she said.

"Crime is out of control, businesses are suffering … however, we really need to keep a lid on being a vigilante — you're not Batman," Ms Benham said.

The ABC has contacted Ms Benham but had not received a response as of the time of publication.

Mallee MP Jade Benham linked the incident to crime concerns. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

Multiple Aboriginal community members have expressed concern for safety in the area, with some saying they are scared to leave their homes.

The ABC understands police have increased patrols in the area in response to the incident.

The boy's family is calling on the government and local representatives to show leadership, particularly around bail laws.

"These are not simply names in a court matter. They are children with families who love them. I saw their fear and pain firsthand, and our families continue to live with the effects," the family statement said.

"I understand that bail is part of the legal process … restrictions involving a driver's licence and a curfew do not feel adequate when two children and their families have experienced such significant fear, distress and trauma.

"I respectfully ask that our concerns be heard and that consideration be given to how the justice system can better protect and support children, victims and their families while criminal proceedings are underway."

World.title: Witness describes the horror of seeing bird flu in native species
World.content:
At Port Macdonnell in South Australia's south-east, a bird's unusual and disturbing behaviour catches the eye of locals.

Warning: This story contains images and video that some readers may find distressing.

On the ground it flaps its wings, turns in circles, cranes its neck and then somersaults.

Loading...

H5N1 bird flu can only be confirmed through testing but after viewing a video of the bird, a veterinarian has told 7.30 its neurological symptoms are consistent with the virus.

"Neurological signs were very obvious including stargazing (opisthotonus), incoordination, and abnormal posture — no signs of seizures or paralysis but that could happen," Wildlife veterinarian and associate professor at Adelaide University Wayne Boardman said.

Infected birds will then die.

Maureen Christie is the secretary of Friends of Shorebirds SE, in South Australia, and has been involved in conserving and tagging birds for research for years.

Now her time is spent documenting the virus's impact on her local area of Carpenter Rocks.

"It makes me like I'm going to just burst into tears any minute," Ms Christie told 7.30.

Maureen Christie is worried about the number of dead birds appearing at Carpenter Rocks. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"You walk onto the beach and there's one dead bird, and two steps on there's another dead bird, and you turn around and take one step the other way and there's another dead bird.

"The crested terns, the ones that I've seen that have been sick, tend to be off by themselves and be fairly still, huddled down, hunched down and looking miserable.

A dead bird on the beach at Carpenter Rocks. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"I've seen two silver gulls sick. And one was throwing its head way back, all out of the way they normally act, and barely able to stay on its feet.

"[It's] absolutely awful because there's nothing you can do about it. They can't be saved.

South Australia's south-east has seen a number of cases of bird flu. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"It's not like a sick or injured bird that can be taken into care and brought back to health. Once these birds have the disease, they're going to die."

The 'list of doom'

Fairy penguins on Phillip Island will be vaccinated for bird flu. (AAP: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

A federal government report dubbed "a list of doom" has warned almost 400 native bird and mammal species are at high to extreme risk from bird flu, including penguins, sea lions and seals and the Tasmanian Devil.

The federal government has committed $2 million to vaccinate vulnerable birds in captivity, along with more than 5,000 penguins on Victoria's Phillip Island and St Kilda.

"Obviously we have some quite unique animals and wildlife in Australia that we are concerned about," Agriculture Minister Julie Collins told 7.30.

"In terms of the funding, the $113 million, over $47 million of that has gone into resilience and improving habitat for those threatened native species."

University of Queensland virologist Kirsty Short said she was concerned about the virus's impact on native birds, based on research which had shown black swans were more susceptible to the virus than white swans.

Loading...

"We hypothesised based on this that Australia's geographic isolation could cause some species to have a restricted immune response because there wasn't that selective pressure, and as a result, being more susceptible to H5N1 than say Northern Hemisphere species," Professor Short said.

" Unfortunately, Australia has a very strong history of extinction. And the thing that I'm concerned about is that this may be the tipping factor that tips a species into extinction. "

It's been almost two months since bird flu was detected in Australia. It's now been found in all six states, including the first suspected positive result in Tasmania on Thursday.

Virologist Kirsty Short says Australia's isolation may mean some native species have "a restricted immune response" to H5N1. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Professor Short told 7.30 that Australia and New Zealand were the "last holdout", with H5N1 having ravaged more than 80 countries worldwide.

Globally, hundreds of millions of poultry have died or been slaughtered because of the virus.

"H5N1, which we often refer to as bird flu … really first emerged in Southern China in 1996," Professor Short said.

"And what happened is that H5N1 then spread around the world, but it continued to evolve."

Farmers fearing the worst

Egg producer Brian Ahmed is preparing for the worst. (ABC News: Nick O'Farrell)

While the virus has been found in wild and native birds in Australia, it's yet to be detected in poultry here. The risk to humans is low.

Professor Short told 7.30 the virus is brutal on poultry.

"Chickens can actually have a lot of swelling and haemorrhaging, and they can die within 24 hours," she said.

Farmers like Victorian egg producer Brian Ahmed are preparing for the worst.

"At the moment we're very strict on who we allow onto the property. We have a fenced off area where all our sheds are and no one's going to go into that section unless they have to," Mr Ahmed told 7.30.

As a caged egg supplier, he said his farm was at less risk than free-range producers.

Brian Ahmed has introduced strict protocols on his chicken farm. (ABC News: Nick O'Farrell)

Inghams has locked down its poultry nationwide and anyone with more than 50 birds in Victoria's coastal or southern areas must keep them indoors.

One sick chicken on a commercial farm would force a cull.

"It is extreme and it's a big cost both emotionally and financially for farmers," Mr Ahmed said.

"This is how we make our living. It's how we support our families. And it's also how we produce food to feed other Australian families."

Breeds could be 'lost for good'

The nation's poultry industry is on high alert. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

Poultry fanciers, like Anne Beaty, are on edge. She has more than 100 birds.

" My birds mean a lot to me. They're part of the family. "

Ms Beaty is secretary of the Victorian Poultry Fanciers Association, a judge and an exhibitor of birds.

Last weekend she helped run a show in Geelong with heightened biosecurity measures. It could be the last for some time.

Anne Beaty is worried rare breeds of birds could be wiped out. (ABC News: Nick O'Farrell)

Poultry exhibits at next month's Royal Adelaide Show and Melbourne Show have been cancelled.

Ms Beaty said poultry fanciers had spent years breeding and developing their flock.

"Some of the breeds of birds are rare and that means there's not many people showing them," she said.

" Now, if those breeds are lost, they're lost for good. That's it. They're done. "

Vaccines have been used in Asia to manage bird flu in poultry, but not in Australia.

A duck at the Geelong poultry show. (ABC News: Nick O'Farrell)

Ms Collins said that's "not something we're ruling out here".

"We're certainly working very closely with industry and with the technical experts on what is viable and feasible," she said.

The federal government has said it will stop testing every dead bird as it was moving to a reporting system based on events.

Professor Short said it is difficult to predict how bird flu will continue to spread across Australia but based on the overseas experience the virus is here to stay.

Australia's first confirmed case of local transmission of H5N1 bird flu was among greater crested terns in South Australia in July. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

"This particular strain of H5N1 seems to be incredibly effective at spreading as well as infecting different species," she said.

"This [strain] first emerged in the Netherlands in 2020 and still now the Netherlands are having outbreaks. So this is not a short-term situation."

A dead bird on the beach at Carpenter Rocks. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

In Carpenter Rocks, Ms Christie was trying to stay positive and hoped whatever the impact on birds, species would eventually bounce back.

"The death toll? It will be what it'll be," she said.

" [But] I can't imagine life without the variety of the animals and plants that we've got. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Chinese state-linked observatory sought NZ site, spy agency says
World.content:
New Zealand's security agency says it has disrupted an attempt by a Chinese state-linked observatory to install satellite-tracking infrastructure in the country, highlighting the case in its annual assessment of an increasingly dangerous espionage environment.

The New Zealand Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS) said Purple Mountain Observatory, an organisation based in China with close ties to the government in Beijing, had sought to install ground-based space infrastructure through a local company that was likely unaware that the equipment could collect intelligence of military value.

Chinese research vessel raises suspicions in Pacific The strange patterns of a Chinese research vessel in Palau's waters have raised suspicions China is gathering intelligence for a potential conflict.

The agency did not identify the New Zealand company or detail how the plans were disrupted.

The warning appeared in the agency's Security Threat Environment 2026 assessment, released today, which said China was the only country New Zealand had detected conducting espionage "at scale".

"Our last report described the threat environment as being the most challenging of recent times," NZSIS Director-General Andrew Hampton said.

" The kinds of malign behaviours and activities we have seen over the past 12 months are proving even more threatening for a country like New Zealand, given its size and location in the South Pacific. "

The Chinese embassy in New Zealand has not responded to a request for comment and the observatory did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

NZSIS said China's intelligence services were the most active espionage threat it faced, while cautioning that the finding should not prevent New Zealand organisations from trading or collaborating with Chinese entities.

It urged an "eyes wide open" approach to overseas business and research ties.

Five Eyes warn of Chinese spies on LinkedIn Australia and its partners in the Five Eyes intelligence alliance warn that Chinese spies are using job platforms to post fake ads to lure recruits with access to sensitive information.

The agency said Beijing's national security laws could compel Chinese individuals and organisations to comply with intelligence-service requests, including by handing over data, intellectual property or system access.

In the Purple Mountain case, NZSIS assessed that any data collected would have been passed to the Chinese government willingly.

New Zealand's location in the South Pacific makes it attractive for ground-based systems that track satellites, space debris and other scientific data, NZSIS said.

It is also a member of the Five Eyes security grouping which includes the US, Britain, Canada and Australia.

NZSIS said foreign states were targeting New Zealand government agencies, companies, universities and researchers for non-public information, innovative technology and intellectual property.

Methods included cyber intrusions, recruitment of insiders, academic partnerships, front companies and commercial intermediaries.

It said geopolitical rivalry, competition over technology and supply chains, foreign interference targeting diaspora communities, and the use of artificial intelligence to spread polarising or deceptive content were compounding risks.

Reuters

World.title: Bird flu threat to endangered native wildlife spurs contingency plans
World.content:
From ferocious devils ambling through the bush to colourful birds found nowhere else in the world, Tasmania is renowned for its unique wildlife.

These animals are now under threat following the detection of the H5N1 bird flu strain in the carcass of a brown skua on the state's north-west coast.

The arrival follows months of careful planning and triggers a suite of protection measures, including increased surveillance and a vaccination program.

Species that gather in dense colonies, scavenge carcasses or already face extinction pressures are being prioritised as authorities work to limit mortalities.

Here is a look at which animals are considered most at risk, and what is being done to protect them.

Tasmanian devil

It is not known how bird flu might affect the Tasmanian devil. (Supplied: Aussie Ark)

One of the biggest unknowns is how the virus will impact the state's most iconic animal — the endangered Tasmanian devil.

As carnivorous marsupials, devils regularly scavenge on the carcasses of other animals, meaning it is almost a certainty some will eventually eat infected birds.

But whether the virus will then infect the devils is still unknown, according to Rachael Alderman from Tasmania's Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE).

"That's an uncertainty but something we're very concerned about so we're watching, monitoring and preparing as much as we can," Dr Alderman said.

"An additional threat is going to add pressure to their safety and long-term survival, so we are worried, but we're not necessarily expecting it to happen."

To help protect the species, work is taking place to strengthen captive populations of Tasmanian devils by reducing disease and boosting genetic diversity.

There is currently no H5 bird flu vaccine for mammals, but Dr Alderman said there was "a lot of work being done" in that space.

Orange-bellied parrot

The critically endangered orange-bellied parrot breeds at Melaleuca in south-west Tasmania. (Supplied: Dejan Stojanovic)

The critically endangered orange-bellied parrot is one of Australia's most threatened bird species, with only 88 detected in the wild last year.

To report sick or dead birds or other animals Call the ​ Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 1800 675 888 ( 24 hours)

Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 24 hours) Use the online bird flu reporting form

Do not touch sick or dead birds or other animals. To report sick or dead wildlife (other than birds), please visit the wildlife health in Tasmania webpage.

Tasmanian Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said H5 bird flu posed a "significant risk" to the species, so the state government was planning to roll out a vaccination program.

Once approved by the state government, the H5 bird flu vaccine will be administered to 350 orange-bellied parrots within a captive breeding centre at Five Mile Beach near Hobart.

"We cannot eliminate the risk entirely, but we're taking action to give our orange-bellied parrots the best possible chance in the event of an outbreak," Mr Barnett said.

Additional protective measures, such as specialised shade cloth infrastructure, will also be implemented at the facility to reduce the risk of disease transmission.

A male orange-bellied parrot at the Five Mile Beach captive breeding centre, where parrots will receive a vaccine. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

It is hoped the vaccination program will begin in September to coincide with parts of the breeding program and sequencing in the captive population.

Australia's Threatened Species commissioner Fiona Fraser said she was "really thrilled" that Tasmania would be looking to run a vaccination program for the orange-bellied parrots.

"Of course, vaccination alone is not sufficient to really build the resilience of our species to H5 bird flu, but it is a very important tool for some of those species," Dr Fraser said.

Little penguin

Little penguins will not receive a vaccine in Tasmania, but work is being done to help protect their habitat. (Wikimedia: JJ Harrison)

Tasmania's coastlines and nearby islands are dotted with colonies of little penguins, which are at risk of experiencing significant mortalities following the arrival of H5 bird flu.

Mr Barnett said while the birds were "much-loved" and "treasured", they were not being considered a priority species for a vaccination program.

This is because of their large population numbers, the fact they are not a threatened species and because of the strict conditions required to receive a permit for the vaccine.

"Two doses are required, separated by a period of one or two weeks, and you need to be able to monitor those individuals after you have vaccinated them," Dr Alderman said.

"We can do orange-bellied parrots because we have the ability to comply really easily with all those conditions; we couldn't do that with little penguins."

Victorian authorities are planning to round up 5,000 little penguins on Phillip Island to administer the H5 bird flu vaccine.

Dr Alderman said the situations were not comparable, as Victoria could meet the permit requirements with the Phillip Island population.

Instead, efforts to preserve little penguin populations in Tasmania will include the removal of weeds on beaches and work to reduce the impact of pests.

Native seabirds

Shy albatross are among the seabirds at high risk from bird flu. (Supplied: Helen_Cunningham)

Wild aquatic birds have undoubtedly been the wildlife group most heavily impacted by the H5 bird flu pandemic as it has spread across the world.

BirdLife Australia senior advisor Sean Dooley said the arrival of the virus in Tasmania was particularly concerning, as it is a "really important migratory shorebird and seabird area".

The state government has identified the shy albatross, the short-tailed shearwater, the white-fronted tern, the fairy and little terns, and the Australasian gannet as species at high risk.

The Australasian gannet is another species identified as being at high risk. (Taubin/flickr.com)

Albatross Island, where about 40 per cent of shy albatross come to breed, is only about 100 kilometres from where the infected brown skua was found, something Mr Dooley said was concerning.

He said terns often suffered "the most severe consequences" during an outbreak of H5 bird flu and that the virus could be "catastrophic" if it hit a breeding colony of gannets.

"It's not only about dealing with the threat of trying to limit the spread of bird flu, it's also making sure that our unique wildlife is in the best position to recover," Mr Dooley said.

"So we need to be able to ensure that colonies of seabirds in particular are free from threats like feral animals or weeds invading their area."

The seasonal harvesting of short-tailed shearwater chicks, known as muttonbirding, is one of the oldest enduring cultural practices for Tasmania's Aboriginal people.

NRE secretary Jason Jacobi said if an outbreak was detected within a colony, the department may work with the Aboriginal community to impose a temporary suspension on muttonbirding.

There are also concerns about the impact bird flu could have on wedge-tailed eagles. (ABC: Chris Lewis)

Some of the other seabirds that Mr Dooley said he was particularly concerned about included the white-bellied sea eagle and the Tasmanian wedge-tailed eagle.

Seals

No vaccine is available for seals. (Supplied: Robert Harcourt)

Neil the seal not immune from bird flu threat Despite his relatively solo lifestyle, Neil the seal may not be isolated from the threat of bird flu.

Some of the most devastating images of the national H5 outbreak were seen on Heard Island in the Southern Ocean, when thousands of baby seals were killed by the virus.

As the deadly strain reaches Tasmania, the state government has identified the Australian and long-nosed fur seals as two species at high risk.

Dr Alderman said this was partly because of the way the seals gathered in large groups, which made it easier for the disease to transmit.

Seals often gather in large numbers, making it easier for the disease to spread. (Supplied: Lisa Byrne)

As they are mammals, there is no vaccine available for seals. However, Dr Fraser said work was being done to build the resilience of wild populations.

The arrival of H5 bird flu in Tasmania is potentially bad news for Neil the seal — a juvenile elephant seal famous for causing havoc on his semi-annual visits to the island.

World.title: Pallister downs McIntosh to claim 200m gold medal at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's freestyle star Lani Pallister has collected gold and silver medals in her arduous opening to the Pan Pacific championships in the United States.

Pallister triumphed in the women's 200m freestyle and then set a personal best when finishing behind American legend Katie Ledecky in the 1500m freestyle in Irvine, California on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Dolphins teammates Sam Short (men's 800m freestyle), Brittany Castelluzzo (women's 200m butterfly) and Ben Armbruster (men's 50m butterfly) also triumphed on the opening night of the Pan Pacs.

The Dolphins won four of 11 gold medals on offer, with Pallister's remarkable year continuing.

Sam Short claimed gold in the men's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Just weeks after winning four Commonwealth Games gold medals in Glasgow, Pallister pipped Canadian ace Summer McIntosh in the 200m final.

The Australian clocked one minute 53.67 seconds — just 0.02s outside her personal best in the event — with McIntosh second in 1:53.86.

About two hours later, Pallister then returned to the pool for the gruelling 1500m freestyle and set a her best time over the distance.

In what was essentially a match race against peerless American great Ledecky, who hasn't lost in the event in 16 years, Pallister put in a gallant effort.

Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: Ex-bishop found to have abused young men at the height of his powers
World.content:
The former Bishop of Broome, who at the peak of his powers was one of the most senior and long-serving Catholic clerics in the country, has been found guilty of sexually abusing young men.

Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, has been on trial accused of sex offences against three young men when he was the Bishop of a remote area of Western Australia three times larger than England.

Christopher Saunders served as the Catholic Bishop of Broome for 25 years. (Supplied)

After a trial that ran for more than three weeks, a District Court jury took almost seven hours to find him guilty of abusing two of those men.

He was convicted of one count of sexual penetration and 12 counts of indecent assault.

Bishop Christopher Saunders meets Pope Francis in 2019. (Supplied)

Saunders was found not guilty of six other charges.

There was no reaction from the former bishop after the verdicts were read out.

The hierarchy of the church The Catholic Church hierarchy is generally in this order: pope, bishops/archbishops, priests, deacons.

Cardinals occupy a special position within the structure.

A bishop is the chief priest of a diocese, which cover multiple churches in a jurisdiction.

Bishops are responsible for the pastoral care of the people in their jurisdiction. Source: perthcatholic.org.au

Vulnerable victims

The victims were young Aboriginal men who lived in the Kimberley, where Indigenous people make up more than 40 per cent of the population.

The assaults happened at various places, including at the Bishop's Catholic church-owned residence in the popular tourist haven of Broome, and at a retreat known as the beach house.

The court had been told of "shirts off" gatherings that Saunders held, supplying alcohol and food to young men wearing only boxer shorts.

The then-bishop would occasionally engage in wrestling and boxing with the men, the court heard.

An aerial view of the retreat showing the 'beach house' in WA's north where some of the offences occurred. (Supplied)

The court had heard Mr Saunders had used his feet to touch young men sexually, grabbed their "privates" and in one instance, engaged in oral sex without consent.

As he chose not to give evidence in his defence, the playing of police interview recordings were the only occasions when the jurors could hear denials from Mr Saunders himself.

The prosecution told the jury Mr Saunders had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men and a "tendency" to act on that interest.

In closing submissions, prosecutor Adam Ebell said while the victims did have criminal histories, the jurors should focus on what they said happened to them at the hands of Saunders, a trusted figure at least one of the men referred to as 'Brother B'.

Prosecutor Adam Ebell encouraged the jury to focus on the testimony of the men. (ABC News: David Weber)

Defence lawyer Tony Hager said his client's behaviour might have been unusual, "boozy" and "sleazy".

But Mr Hager said Saunders wasn't on trial for inviting young Aboriginal men over to have a drink, or for using church funds to buy alcohol, or for taking alcohol to a dry community.

Defence lawyer Tony Hager described the behaviour as "sleazy". (ABC News: David Weber )

He told the jury his client "wasn't on trial in Rome" for not adhering to a code of conduct, or "standing before the Pope" trying to justify his pastoral care as he was not on trial "as a representative of the Catholic Church".

Mr Hager suggested the memories of the three complainants may have been affected by alcohol use, especially given the passage of time since the alleged events.

Bishop taken into custody

It can now be revealed that on the first day of the trial, without the jury present, the prosecution told the court four charges, involving a much younger alleged victim, would be discontinued.

They were three counts of indecent dealing with a child under 13, and one count of sexual penetration of a child under 13.

The bishop was well known in WA's north, pictured here sitting for an interview with the ABC in the 2010's. (ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins)

The incidents were alleged to have occurred when Mr Saunders was the Bishop of Broome.

Saunders will next face court on September 21 for a sentencing hearing.

He made no application for bail and has been remanded in custody.

'Deeply sorry'

In a statement, Bishop of Broome Tim Norton apologised to victims, saying the diocese was "deeply sorry for the hurt they have experienced".

"We are sorry for the shame they have endured," he wrote.

"We are sorry that it has taken so long for their voices to be heard and for their pain to be acknowledged."

World.title: Virgin plane aborts take-off as Qantas plane crosses Sydney runway
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesAviation Virgin plane aborts take-off as Qantas plane crosses Sydney runway Chris Zappone August 13, 2026 — 6:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Investigators are probing the third safety incident at Sydney Airport in less than three weeks after a Virgin plane was force to abort take-off after discovering a Qantas plane on its runway. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau said it is investigating a runway incursion and rejected take-off of Virgin Australia flight VA555 from Sydney to Perth and Qantas flight QF728 from Sydney to Ayers Rock Airport. A Virgin 737 and a Qantas 737 in Sydney. Bloomberg The incident, which occurred shortly after 10am on August 9, involved two Boeing 737s. Air traffic control cleared the Virgin Australia 737 “for a full-length take-off” on runway 34L, the ATSB said. “As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed the Qantas 737 begin to cross the runway ahead of them from taxiway Lima.”



“The Qantas crew reported having received a clearance from ATC to cross the runway,” the ATSB said. The Virgin Australia crew then reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop on the runway, the ATSB said. Air traffic control then broadcast a cancellation of the take-off clearance. Flightradar24 shows the Virgin 737 beginning its take-off as the Qantas 737 crosses runway 34L at Sydney Airport. Flightradar24 Once the Qantas 737 was clear of the active runway, the Virgin Australia 737 was re-cleared to take-off. The incident comes after two other near-misses on the ground at Sydney Airport, both under ATSB investigation, as well as a series of delays.



Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp had been summoned by Transport Minister Catherine King to assure that operations move smoothly in Sydney over the next month. Airservices Australia is in the process of bolstering its roster of air traffic controllers in Sydney, which are in short supply and frequently forced to cover shifts. A spokesperson for Virgin Australia said: “We reported the matter to the ATSB in line with our safety procedures and will support its investigation. We take the safety of our guests and crew extremely seriously.” A spokesperson for Qantas said: “Our aircraft was cleared to proceed following instructions from Air Traffic Control and we will support the ATSB in the investigation.” Airservices Australia said it is working with the ATSB to “investigate recent incidents involving aircraft moving on the ground at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport”. “Safety is Airservices’ top priority and we are committed to working with all stakeholders including airlines, ground handlers, regulators and airport operators to keep the travelling public safe.”



It’s understood the air traffic controller cancelled the take-off clearance of the Virgin plane within four seconds of the initial clearance after seeing the previously cleared Qantas aircraft crossing the runway. On Sunday morning at Sydney airport there was a near ground collision involving a Jetstar A320 and a Qatar Airways 777 that was under tow. Nick Scali is investigating a cyberattack that led the furniture seller to take its systems offline and left frustrated customers in the dark about missing or delayed deliveries. Following enquiries from this masthead, the company confirmed to the ASX it had been hit by a “security incident” and was working on bringing parts of its network back online. “We note that the company is continuing to complete sales orders and deliveries. Our response times to customers are currently slower than normal,” Nick Scali said in a statement. Nick Scali chief executive Anthony Scali has said the company is contacting customers about orders after being hit by a security attack. Louie Douvis There has been no evidence of unauthorised access to customer data, and has referred the matter to Federal Police and the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the statement said.



Nick Scali boss Anthony Scali said the incident happened “about mid-last week” and that staff were referring to manual records to get in touch with customers whose orders had been impacted. “The system got attacked, like everyone else,” Scali told this masthead. “We kept orders going, but I guess the recovery was not as easy as we first thought. Everything’s offline. We’re bringing some components back up now … Shouldn’t be too long.” Nick Scali’s main website or social media accounts didn’t contain any information about the outage. Customers would have to navigate to the “My account” page to find a notification of the incident. “We’re currently experiencing a system outage with recovery underway,” the notification states. “We’re still operating as normal and delivering, however, certain processes have been slowed down so response times have increased. We ask for your patience during this period, and we will get back to you.”



Melbourne resident and Nick Scali customer Bill Bariamis said he had not received any communication about the outage after staying home last Monday for the expected delivery of a dining table, which never arrived. He received a notification advising delivery had been rescheduled to Wednesday, but it didn’t arrive on that day either. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications ‘Accountability rests with me’: Telstra boss rakes in $6.8m but Triple Zero outage costs her Bariamis visited Nick Scali’s Frankston store, where he bought the table, and was told by apologetic store staff that there had been a “major outage of computers and telephones for the last week”, but the employees did not have any further details to share. “There are people all over the country waiting around for stuff,” he said. “No delivery, no update, no information, no nothing.” The $1.4 billion retailer, which has 132 stores around the world, on Friday reported a 22.1 per cent jump in full-year net profits to $75.7 million, but made no mention of any security incident.



A customer service representative contacted through Nick Scali’s phone line earlier on Thursday said the company had suffered a “nationwide outage” impacting the company mainframe that would take “a couple of weeks” to resolve. “We can’t get emails or phone calls to stores, and we can’t retrieve our orders,” the representative said. “That’s all the information I have.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: From bowled out for 54 in a warm-up game, to a day-one stranglehold: Bangladesh stun Australia
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket From bowled out for 54 in a warm-up game, to a day-one stranglehold: Bangladesh stun Australia Daniel Brettig August 13, 2026 — 6:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: Australia’s first day of Test cricket since January left them badly shown up by Bangladesh and will make the brutal 20 matches in 12 months look like a tour of duty set to end more than a few careers. Watched by a well-oiled Top-End crowd of 5233 at Marrara Stadium, this was a sobering day for the Australians, who now face a stiff task to fight their way back into the match – an unimaginable notion when the tourists were bowled out for 54 in their warm-up game. Hasan Mahmud waves the red Kookaburra to the crowd after his stellar bowling effort. Getty Images At the same time, the sluggishness on display will only enhance the suspicions of many that the selectors may have been better off including one or two younger, hungry names in the squad to provide a sense of forward-thinking. “Right now, there are a couple of chinks in the armour and the selectors decided to stick with what they know,” former captain Ricky Ponting said on Seven. “At the end of last season, I thought the time was right now to blood a couple of youngsters into these two Test matches.”



The sense of an Australian team far from full-throttle began when Pat Cummins oddly chose to bat first on a seaming pitch, and carried on through a poor first innings total of 198 and a spiky reply by a Bangladesh side (1-96) that are here chasing respect. None of Jake Weatherald, Marnus Labuschagne or Cameron Green did anything to quell growing questions about their places in the team with a trio of low scores, while Travis Head, Alex Carey and Beau Webster were unable to mount another relief operation. Ebadot Hossain celebrates the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne in the first Test in Darwin. Getty Images Not even top scorer Steve Smith, who scrounged his way to 71 while surviving several chances, was able to summon his best against a Bangladesh side that offered a facsimile of a solid Sheffield Shield bowling attack on a well-grassed and slow surface that rewarded accuracy over pace. “Not sure [if batting first was a factor]. We won the toss and decided to,” Smith said. “I don’t know any other reasoning. I didn’t hear too much to be honest, maybe it’s one to look at.



It was hard work for Alex Carey, Steve Smith and the Australian batters on day one. Getty Images “Yesterday guys thought the wicket was rock-hard. We turned up this morning, and it was a bit tacky, I think just from the dew, potentially. It definitely hardened up as the day went on, but it will be interesting to see if there’s that same dew tomorrow morning.” Smith also admitted he thought he had edged one behind on seven in the morning session, but Ultra Edge technology showed nothing on replay, so Bangladesh’s appeal was denied. “You’ve got to take it sometimes,” Smith said with a laugh. “Maybe I didn’t nick it, but I certainly felt something. If I’d been given out I was going to walk off.” Hasan Mahmud bowled splendidly to claim 6-55, well-supported by Taskin Ahmed (2-55) and Ebadot Hossain (2-39). Ponting said Australia’s innings had been pockmarked by too many repeat mistakes.



“I think that was pretty difficult conditions, the batting,” Ponting said. “I think we were all surprised that Australia chose to bat this morning. Looking at the surface, there was some grass on it. It was nice and hard. So I think we all expected some seam movement and it to be hard work for the batters. “But what I’ve seen so far today is just the same mistakes being made again, particularly by some of our top-order players. [There was] almost sometimes an over-intent to try and score the balls that aren’t quite there, hence Weatherald’s dismissal. “And you look at Marnus and there’s a lack of intent to try and score, which builds pressure on him and keeps the bowlers in the game, and then he gets out the same way that we’ve seen a lot over the last couple of years.” Mitchell Starc’s first ball swung threateningly past the outside edge, but what followed was often too short and not threatening the stumps. This was compounded when Nathan Lyon looked hesitant going for a high, swirling chance from backward point and failed even to get a finger on it. View post on X



By the close of play, Cummins and company were only 102 runs in credit with one wicket to their names: it is already a long way back. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Sorry for the pain this has caused’: Gardner’s public apology to her ex as CA stands by the vice captain Walking out to bat under overcast, muggy skies, Weatherald and Head got to 45 without looking secure. Weatherald’s ambitious edged drive at a ball seaming away from him opened things up, and a steady decline followed. Head dragged one on from round the wicket, Labuschagne fenced indecisively at a ball on sixth stump, and in the last over before lunch Green hooked an impulsive six before needlessly flicking a straighter ball to mid-wicket. Smith and Carey were little troubled in adding 55, but mid-afternoon drinks broke the wicketkeeper’s cocoon of concentration, and when Webster was also bowled, a suboptimal total became more or less inevitable.



Australia may have harboured notions of blowing Bangladesh away with the ball, but Tanzid Hasan and Mominul Haque stood fast. This game, and this year, are not going to be easy for Cummins’ creaking terminators. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Investigators are probing the third safety incident at Sydney Airport in less than three weeks after a Virgin plane was force to abort take-off after discovering a Qantas plane on its runway. Air traffic control cleared the Virgin Australia 737 “for a full-length take-off” on runway 34L, the ATSB said. “As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed the Qantas 737 begin to cross the runway ahead of them from taxiway Lima.”



“The Qantas crew reported having received a clearance from ATC to cross the runway,” the ATSB said. The Virgin Australia crew then reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop on the runway, the ATSB said. Air traffic control then broadcast a cancellation of the take-off clearance. Flightradar24 shows the Virgin 737 beginning its take-off as the Qantas 737 crosses runway 34L at Sydney Airport. Flightradar24 Once the Qantas 737 was clear of the active runway, the Virgin Australia 737 was re-cleared to take-off. The incident comes after two other near-misses on the ground at Sydney Airport, both under ATSB investigation, as well as a series of delays.



Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp had been summoned by Transport Minister Catherine King to assure that operations move smoothly in Sydney over the next month. Airservices Australia is in the process of bolstering its roster of air traffic controllers in Sydney, which are in short supply and frequently forced to cover shifts. A spokesperson for Virgin Australia said: “We reported the matter to the ATSB in line with our safety procedures and will support its investigation. We take the safety of our guests and crew extremely seriously.” A spokesperson for Qantas said: “Our aircraft was cleared to proceed following instructions from Air Traffic Control and we will support the ATSB in the investigation.” Airservices Australia said it is working with the ATSB to “investigate recent incidents involving aircraft moving on the ground at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport”. “Safety is Airservices’ top priority and we are committed to working with all stakeholders including airlines, ground handlers, regulators and airport operators to keep the travelling public safe.”



It’s understood the air traffic controller cancelled the take-off clearance of the Virgin plane within four seconds of the initial clearance after seeing the previously cleared Qantas aircraft crossing the runway. On Sunday morning at Sydney airport there was a near ground collision involving a Jetstar A320 and a Qatar Airways 777 that was under tow. Two airport workers were stood down, and minister King warned Airservices Australia CEO Rob Sharp that: “The delays and disruptions we have seen at Sydney Airport over the last three days have been unacceptable and have caused significant disruption to passengers, staff and airlines.” Two weeks earlier, on July 27, a QantasLink flight and a Qantas flight were involved in a near miss on the tarmac in Sydney. “I actually forgot how to hold the bat for my first 30 balls. I’m not going to lie,” Smith told Fox Cricket, referencing his lack of match practice leading into this clash.

“Then I figured it out and felt really good. So, yeah, obviously I didn’t have many partners come with me today, unfortunately. But that happens sometimes.”
